articles.title: How green is Europe's urban public transport? A data-driven reality check
articles.summary: Greener buses and cleaner fleets are reshaping public transport across Europe. But are cities moving fast enough to meet their zero-emission goals?

image.caption: Electric buses, like this one in the Belgian capital of Brussels, are becoming increasingly common in European public transport systemsImage: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: An electric plug icon on their windows makes them easy to spot in cities like Brussels and Madrid. Quietly navigating the streets, electric buses have become an increasingly common sight on Europe's streets in recent years.

Michela Le Pira, assistant professor of transportation at Italy's University of Catania says removing tailpipe emissions — the gases and particles generated when a combustion vehicle is running — might be "the easiest strategy to improve public transport."

Most Europeans live in urban settings, and road transport has a negative impact on air quality. In 2023, almost 300,000 deaths across the EU were caused by air pollution levels that exceeded the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommended thresholds.

Of all fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations in European urban areas, about 14% come from road transport, which includes public but also private and freight transport. Additionally, towns and cities account for nearly a quarter of the European Union's transport greenhouse gases emissions (GHG).

DW and the European Data Journalism Network evaluated over a decade of data from more than 100 reports and sources on public transit and the emissions it causes, and identified 148 sustainability commitments by local authorities and transport operators in 33 cities across Europe. The analysis focuses on motorized mass transit, leaving out bikes and pedestrians as well as taxis, shared vehicles and e-scooters.
More electric buses, thanks to EU funds
The EU wants to become the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. A key part of that plan is cutting transport-related GHG emissions by 90% from 1990 levels.

As DW's analysis shows, Copenhagen is the only EU capital that has almost electrified its entire bus fleet — their vehicles do not have combustion engines and therefore do not produce tailpipe emissions. In cities like Rome, Lisbon and Nicosia, more than 90% of buses still run on diesel, and metros and trams account for less than 10% of their public transport fleet.

Although cars still dominate European streets, "electric buses are one way to reduce local air pollution," said Martin Baierl, data analyst with Transport & Environment, an advocacy non-profit for clean transport.
EU funds enabled many cities to increase their electric and alternative fuel bus fleets from 2021 on.

Electric buses comprise 20% of the total fleet in EU capitals and selected cities. Their number increased by 55% between 2021 and 2025 — equivalent to 1,234 more such vehicles on the road. The number of diesel-only buses has been declining since then, although they still outnumber those running on alternative fuel.
Slow road to sustainability in some cities

In addition to decarbonizing the bus fleet and helping to reduce air pollution, embracing electric models can help to lower noise and public transport operating costs. All the more so if the city produces its own electricity, explains Baierl. However, the outlay for e-buses is higher than for diesel models. In 20 out of the 31 cities with data to analyze, over 50% of the bus fleet is made up of traditional vehicles.

Brussels, for example, was an early adopter of moving away from traditional diesel-powered buses, switching to hybrids instead. Now the Belgian capital is in the process of electrifying its fleet, but at a slower pace. "It's not easy to know what the right technology will be at the end," Baierl said.
Another example are hydrogen-powered buses, which also produce zero-emissions but are more costly to operate than their electric counterparts.
Many cities have not fully committed to zero-emissions despite EU targets
Transportation is the only major sector where greenhouse gas emissions remain above 1990 levels, despite the EU's ambition of a 90% reduction by 2050.

On average, public transport — including buses, trams and metros — is used for more than a quarter of trips in the ten largest EU capitals, according to recent data from the non-profit group Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP). In Stockholm, the share is 49%, while in the smaller Slovenian capital of Ljubljana, it's 11%. DW analysis of transport sustainability pledges reveals that only four cities have explicitly committed to achieving zero-emissions in buses or all public transport.
Rail transport is climate-friendly, but scarce

Yannis Papadimitriou lives 85 kilometers (about 53 miles) away from Athens, the EU capital with the highest air pollution mortality risk. He travels to work by commuter rail, a means of transport he'd like to see promoted more.
"For me it is a very conscious choice to use electric public transport, especially trains, which are the safest, most environmentally friendly and quickest way of transport."
Though trains, trams and metros run on electricity, there are more buses within city boundaries, and in many urban areas the majority still run on diesel.
Public transport's emissions go beyond the tailpipe

In Northern Europe, 15 kilometers away from Copenhagen, Poul Kattler also used to commute to work. He is now retired and takes the bus more frequently with his grandchildren. Despite Copenhagen having an almost completely fossil-fuel-free public transport system (only one bus runs on biomethane), the metro expansion, which is responding to the city's growth, comes with its own set of concerns.

"The whole construction phase [of the new metro line] is extremely environmentally demanding," Kattler said. If the construction emissions are considered, "the CO2 balance would be very poor for the metro now."
But in the long run, the benefits of a new metro line in reducing CO2 emissions outweigh its construction-related emissions, Le Pira said.

Combustion or exhaust emissions are not the only way transport pollutes the air and the environment. Indirect emissions, like those coming from electricity generation or fuel production, add to transport's CO2 footprint. Brakes and wheels release non-exhaust particle matter when wagons or vehicles slow down.

Since 1992, buses and any vehicle running on fossil fuels in the EU have been subject to stricter emissions standards. Fine particle emissions from buses and heavy-duty vehicles had dropped by 92% in 2022 according to the European Environment Agency. Yet overall road transport non-exhaust emissions from tire wear have increased 58% in two decades, as cars have become heavier.
Shifting from cars to a multimodal transport system
With a few exceptions, EU member states are not close to cutting greenhouse gas transport emissions by 90%, as envisioned by the EU's 2050 target.
Zero-emission public transport is one step toward decarbonizing transport in cities and meeting GHG reduction goals. The next challenge is to get people out of their cars.
"If we talk about sustainable mobility in general and not only clean public transport, the main problem is the model shift from private cars to public transport," Le Pira said.
On average, private automobiles account for more than a third of transport in the largest EU capitals, according to CDP data.
Cheaper ticket prices for groups, like students, and disincentives for car use, such as low-emission zones, are two complementary ways of attracting more passengers while reducing private transport.

In her research work, Le Pira investigates how public transport can be more efficient and appealing for city dwellers, for example, by combining transport modes where people step off their bikes and onto a train. This kind of solution could be particularly relevant for small cities "where cars are still the main transport mode".
Places with good public transport draw people in.
"Cities where not everybody has to use a car are just more livable," Baierl said.
Fact check: Eva Lopez
DW's data team contributed research to this project.
For data, code and methodology behind this analysis, see this GitHub repository. More data-driven stories from DW can be found here.

This project is a collaboration among several media outlets in the European Data Journalism Network in context of Chat Europe. Project lead: DW. Contributing partners: Voxeurop, Denik Referendum, EUrologus, OBC Transeuropa.

articles.title: ABC reporter could face disciplinary action over opinion piece, journalists’ union says
articles.summary: Opinion piece by head of union Michael Slezak sparks disagreement with new ABC director of news, Simon Robinson

blocks.text: ABC management has refused to rule out disciplinary action against a journalist and union office-holder for writing an opinion piece for the Australian Financial Review, according to the Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA).
The award-winning ABC climate journalist, Michael Slezak, had an article published last week in Nine’s financial newspaper in his capacity as federal president of MEAA.
The AFR described Slezak, who is also head of the ABC house committee, as federal president of media at the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance and an ABC journalist.

The article was about a proposal by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic) to restrict journalists from accessing information such as the home address and date of birth of company directors, an issue the union is campaigning on.

Last week Slezak was called to a meeting with the new ABC director of news, Simon Robinson, and the head of digital and national news, Lee Glendinning, to discuss his adherence to the ABC’s external work policy.
Robinson was handpicked by the ABC managing director, Hugh Marks, before the incumbent news chief Justin Stevens was asked to resign in May. The former Reuters executive joined the ABC in September.
In a letter to ABC union members on Monday, the media union claimed Slezak was being targeted for defending press freedom in his capacity as an elected union office-holder.
“Championing our right to information is something we expect Michael to do and be allowed to do without hindrance,” MEAA said.
A spokesperson for the ABC said the guidelines for external work and public comment were important in protecting the reputation of the ABC.
“The Director of News is meeting with staff to ensure there is a clear and consistent understanding of how the guidelines should be applied and upheld.”

The union’s relationship with Marks has been fraught since more than 2,000 staff walked off the job for a 24-hour strike, forcing ABC services across TV, radio and digital to use BBC content and repeat programming.
Marks was publicly critical of the enterprise bargaining process.
after newsletter promotion
The union claims management refused to rule out disciplinary action including dismissal against Slezak at the meeting.

“Simon and Lee raised the possibility that Michael may have breached the ABC’s external work policy and code of conduct,” the union said. “They refused to rule out disciplinary action, including dismissal.”
The union says Slezak did not need to seek approval for the article because he has an agreement with the ABC which permits him to engage in public comment on behalf of journalists in his MEAA role.
The union has called on Marks and Robinson to confirm Slezak will not face disciplinary action in an open letter signed by 197 ABC union members as of Monday afternoon.

“We see this as an attack on our right to work collectively through our union, a hindrance to our delegates doing the work they are legally entitled to do, and an obstruction to journalists in our industry fulfilling their duty to uphold and champion press freedom,” the letter says.
Union members will meet on Tuesday to discuss a collective response.

articles.title: ‘What planet is she on?’: the Seekers take aim at CPAC over use of I am Australian
articles.summary:
The carnival is over for use of Australian band’s song they say was played without permission at conservative conference

  • Get our

blocks.text: A member of legendary Australian band the Seekers has taken aim at a conference featuring Pauline Hanson for using a classic song, confirming no permission had been granted.

Bruce Woodley said the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) featured I Am Australian without approval, while the song’s co-author revealed Hanson had been previously threatened with legal action over its potential use.
I Am Australian was sung as part of CPAC’s opening ceremony in Brisbane on Saturday, after renditions of the national anthem and Waltzing Matilda.
The song – originally co-written by Woodley and the Bushwackers’ Dobe Newton in 1987 – was also advertised as part of the official conference program agenda.
Woodley and Newton lambasted CPAC organisers, saying the song about unity in diversity was at odds with the anti-immigration views expressed at the conference.
“No permission was either sought or given by me for the use of my song,” Woodley said on Monday.
The song’s theme is encapsulated in its line: “We are one, but we are many, and from all the lands of earth we come”.
After the song’s performance, speakers including Hanson and the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, condemned what they called “mass immigration”.
“I would absolutely never endorse the use of the song associated with those purposes,” Newton said.
He said when Hanson tried to use the song in a previous election campaign, he and Woodley threatened her with legal action.
“We said to each other ‘what planet is she on’?” Newton said.
“Bruce and I got a friend of ours to write a furious solicitor’s letter threatening to sue her, and she actually changed her mind.”
He said that during the 2023 voice to parliament referendum, both the yes and no campaigns approached he and Woodley to use the song.
Both were denied.
Mark Callaghan, leader of the band Ganggajang and a long-serving board member of copyright management organisations APRA-AMCOS, said CPAC’s unauthorised use of the song was illegal.
“The bottom line is permission must be sought and approved for any public performance, especially in that political context,” he said.
However, he said enforcement was “like playing whack-a-mole”, with his song Sounds of Then (This is Australia) frequently misused for commercial and political purposes without permission.

“We are finding it’s a real problem all over the internet because people put up political posts and then add Sounds of Then, or I Am Australian or (Icehouse’s) Great Southern Land and implying some sort of connection.”
CPAC organisers have been contacted for comment.

The 1997 recording of I Am Australian by late Seekers singer Judith Durham, Air Supply’s Russell Hitchcock and Yothu Yindi leader, the late Dr M Yunupingu, has become an Australian standard, added to the National Film and Sound Archive registry in 2023.
It was used with permission by the Australian Republican Movement in radio and television advertisements during the 1999 referendum.
It is also regularly used in major national and sporting events.

articles.title: UK students call for school uniforms to be banned in pornography
articles.summary: Short skirts, knee-high socks, white blouses: Girls' school uniform items are widely used as costumes in pornographic videos. As students experience harassment, a group wants to change that.

image.caption: School uniforms are common in dozens of countries worldwideImage: Sven Simon/IMAGO

blocks.text: Aylin and Mae, both age 15, are members of their school's Little Feminist Book Club in Bicester, Oxfordshire, England.
During a group discussion, the club learned that teenagers at other schools were trying to have the sale of school uniforms banned in sex shops.
Schoolgirl costumes are also widely used in pornographic videos.

"All of us unanimously agreed. We wanted to take it a step further; we wanted to ban school uniform from all pornography," Aylin told DW. As a result, they started a petition to raise awareness of the issue.

Many of their fellow students, as the petition states, have already had unpleasant experiences while wearing their uniforms. Some reported being harassed as early as the age of 11. Many of these experiences had left them feeling frightened, ashamed and insecure. "I don't wear my school uniform outside of school," said Mae. "I don't like wearing it out."
One in three schoolgirls reports harassment

In their petition, the girls also refer to a 2018 report by the charity Plan International. According to a survey in the report, 35% of the 1,004 respondents aged 14 to 21 had experienced unwanted sexual attention while wearing a school uniform. Eight percent said they had been filmed or photographed by a stranger without their permission, or that someone had taken a photo under their school skirt, known as "upskirting."

"Something that should actually be innocent, something that is supposed to symbolize a community, has now become discredited in society," says Mae. "And our perception of what a school uniform represents has been distorted by this disgusting media."

blocks.caption: School uniforms are also iconic symbols of Japanese cultureImage: Michael Bihlmayer/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance

blocks.text: School uniforms often mandatory

School uniforms are common in many countries around the world. They are meant to make class and financial divides less visible, which is also supposed to prevent bullying while strengthening a community feeling.
In the UK, uniforms are mandatory at almost all schools and preschools, which means essentially all children between the ages of 4 to 16 wear them.
Outside school, children have no way to escape unwanted attention.
"We just want to prevent people from thinking about children and school uniforms in that way," says Mae. "Hopefully, we'll be able to actually turn the ban into legislation."

Until that happens, they still have a long way to go, but the girls are optimistic. As of October 5, 2026, the petition has garnered more than 24,000 signatures. Thanks to an article in the English newspaper The Times, it's also gotten plenty of attention.
Now, Mae and Aylin hope to get parliament to debate the issue. Two MPs have already voiced their support.

But the girls also know some people believe longer skirts are the solution. "I believe that's wrong," explains Aylin. "We shouldn't blame the victims. We should blame those who think it is acceptable to sexualize them."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Diesel prices drop by P3/L; gasoline, kerosene rise over P1/L
articles.summary: Another round of mixed fuel price adjustments is set to take effect this week, with diesel prices set to roll back while gasoline and kerosene prices rise.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 3:16pm

Motorists line up at a gasoline station on March 1, 2026, two days before the scheduled fuel price hikes, as domestic pump prices are expected to rise amid escalating tensions between Iran and Israel, which have pushed up global oil and gasoline costs.
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — Another round of mixed fuel price adjustments is set to take effect this week, with diesel prices set to roll back while gasoline and kerosene prices rise.
The Department of Energy (DOE) announced the following changes on Monday, October 12:

items: Diesel - down by P3.01 per liter
Gasoline - up by P1.56 per liter
Kerosene - up by P1.77 per liter

blocks.text: The adjustments will take effect on Tuesday morning, October 13, and will remain in effect until Monday next week, October 19.
Last week, an uneven fuel price movement was also implemented, with diesel prices dropping by P1.30 per liter, while gasoline rose by P1.93 per liter and kerosene by P3.30 per liter.
Price influence

The energy department explained that several factors affected this week’s price movements, including China’s export suspension, the availability of middle distillates, and recent global diesel supply relief measures.

The DOE said that while all oil products are affected by China’s recent announcement on the temporary suspension of refined petroleum product exports, recent international agreements have contributed to the rollback in diesel prices.
“Itong diesel kasi may malaking developments dito, positive developments,” DOE Oil Industry and Management Bureau Director Rino Abad said in a press briefing on Monday.
(“There are major, positive developments in diesel [supplies]”)

Among these developments aimed at easing the global diesel shortage, according to the DOE, was the agreement reached by G7 member countries at their meeting on October 2 to immediately release 100 million barrels of petroleum supplies, particularly diesel.
Another was the agreement between the United States and Russia to immediately release 2.25 million barrels of Russian diesel to the US and global markets this October.

This will be followed by 3.75 million barrels in November, an additional 7.5 million barrels in the following months, and a potential additional 7.5 million barrels, depending on the capacity of refineries to process crude oil, according to the DOE.

Meanwhile, the upward price movement for kerosene has been attributed to its sensitivity to the availability and cost of middle distillates, a broader category of fuels that includes diesel and jet fuel.

“The G7 and US-Russia agreement could help ease the global diesel shortage, however, without the same emphasis on the release of additional supply for gasoline and kerosene, prices are expected to remain elevated for these products,” the DOE said.

articles.title: Ukraine says Russia violated Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ – Europe live
articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Kyiv power plant among the facilities hit after US president claims ‘energy ceasefire’, while Kremlin yet to confirm any deal

blocks.text: Ukraine says Russia violated Trump's 'energy ceasefire'
We are restarting our live coverage of the latest developments in Europe after Donald Trump’s announcement of what he called an energy ceasefire in the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Sunday evening that Russian strikes hit Ukrainian energy facilities despite the US president having claimed both sides had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy infrastructure.

In a post on X, Zelenskyy said a drone had hit a Kyiv power plant on Sunday, leading to power outages in the Ukrainian capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on a power plant in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, adding: “Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day”, referring to a type of Iranian-made drone commonly used in the conflict.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he was caught by surprise by Trump’s ceasefire announcement. Photograph: Dan Bashakov/AP

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Russian ⁠attacks killed six people ⁠in two Ukrainian ⁠cities ​on Sunday, including a strike ⁠on a grocery store in Kharkiv, ​where ‌three people died ‌and 20 were ‌injured, Ukrainian officials said. Two children were ‌among the injured, the regional governor said. In western ​Ukraine, ‌a Russian strike ​killed ​three people, officials ​said.

On Sunday morning Trump had announced that “effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine”. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social platform, without further details.

Zelenskyy expressed surprise at the announcement, saying the deal was “news to me”, while Russia has still not confirmed its agreement. Zelenskyy said on Telegram yesterday that: “Ukraine is ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure – and we count on the same readiness from Russia.”

Reflecting a broad skepticism, the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said this morning that the bloc would welcome a truce but only “when it holds”. “We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it,” Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers.
In other developments:

items: Nato Supreme Allied Cmdr Europe Alexus Grynkewich is due to deliver a warning to Russia at a security conference in Warsaw over the alliance’s ability to counter any attack from Moscow.
The Lithuanian ⁠foreign minister Kestutis ​Budrys said the EU should designate the Russian ‌intelligence agency GRU ​as ⁠a ​terrorist organisation.
The Nobel memorial prize in economics, the final award in this year’s cycle, will be announced at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm from 10.45am UK time.

Trump’s surprise ceasefire announcement came two days after he announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel fuel – temporarily lifting US sanactions – prompting outrage from Ukraine and its European allies, who said it would embolden Moscow.

The Trump administration is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times has quoted officials in Europe as saying. They said the US was lobbying European capitals and Kyiv in an attempt to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries.

blocks.caption: Luke Harding

The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.

Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.

The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. articles.title: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality

Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his…

blocks.text: Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops against the Picts and Scots, but a theory that he also established a military camp near Frenni Fawr hill in Wales has so far been based on folklore.
Now fourth-century coins, among other finds at a newly identified Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, suggest the medieval tale was rooted in reality, to the excitement of archaeologists.

The fort was discovered by Dr Mark Merrony, a leading Roman specialist at the University of Oxford. He heads an excavation that is bringing to life a story about Magnus Maximus, as told in the Mabinogion, a collection of medieval epic tales of myth, magic and miracles.

Merrony expressed excitement that this landscape held the only Roman military site close to where the Mabinogion places the emperor. “If Magnus Maximus was there, there must have been an army there,” he said.

blocks.caption: Mark Merrony next to the site of the fort’s headquarters building. Photograph: Mark Merrony

blocks.text: “It’s such a remote area but the tale mentions the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which is where this site is. The presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help unlock the mystery of a Mabinogion legend that has endured for nearly 1,700 years.”

In The Dream of Macsen Wledig, medieval storytellers used the emperor’s name in Welsh in recounting his rise to power. They described how on his military manoeuvres, he pitched his camp at Frenni Fawr, the 395-metre (1,300ft) easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills.

There had been no archaeological evidence for a Roman marching camp or fort on the summit of the Frenni Fawr or below it until now. Merrony discovered it about 2 miles (3.5km) south-west of the summit in 2024. Satellite imagery had shown a convincing outline in an overgrown field and, shortly after visiting it, his eye was caught by a Roman tile, which turned out to be the first of many.
With financial support from Oxford University and crowdfunding, one of several planned excavations has just finished, confirming his theory of the site and its significance.

blocks.caption: Frenni Fawr hill in the Preselis.   Photograph: Mark Merrony

blocks.text: Merrony said that before the dig, his brother, Nick, had jokingly asked him to find a couple of coins to prove the Magnus Maximus theory. “He came back and said ‘well, are these any good?’ I said ‘you’ve got to be kidding me’. He’d found two coins dating from the late 4th century.
“It is fascinating to consider that the two coins may be linked to the tale of Macsen Wledig – Magnus Maximus – in the Mabinogion, the Welsh equivalent of the Odyssey.”

Merrony is a leading specialist in the Romano-British period. His previous discoveries include two Roman villas, at Ford in Pembrokeshire and at Cutteslowe in Oxfordshire. He identified a Roman road along the southern shoulder of the Preselis in 2022, challenging assumptions that the Romans did not venture far into Wales.

His research will appear in Antiqvvs, a quarterly magazine dedicated to archaeology, ancient art and history. Magnus Maximus will also feature in Merrony’s forthcoming book, titled Lives of the Roman Emperors: From Augustus to Romulus Augustulus.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A tile fragment discovered at the site. Photograph: Mark Merrony

blocks.text: Measuring 180 by 150 metres, the fort is on a slope with a commanding view of the surrounding landscape. It is likely to have held about 500 troops, and its discovery overturns assumptions that the area’s Indigenous Celtic tribe was on peaceful terms with the Roman invaders.
It has “a characteristic playing-card form, with rounded corners” and a perpendicular road, Merrony said.

Finds at the site so far include an unusual iron stylus, many pottery shards, large quantities of Roman tiles and extensive compacted clay floors, a common feature on Roman military sites. Even rut marks left by wagons have been preserved.
The geophysical survey confirmed the presence of a rectangular building in the middle of the enclosure and a larger rectangular building immediately to the south.
“This arrangement is consistent with the placement of a headquarters building orientated east and thereby ‘facing the enemy’, and a commander’s house,” Merrony said.

articles.title: Teens at Sydney private religious school made to share beds with teachers, inquiry hears
articles.summary:
Former student says nothing untoward happened to her during stays but tells NSW parliamentary inquiry culture of Redeemer Baptist School left much to ‘untangle’ as an adult

  • Get our…

blocks.text: Teens at a private religious school were made to share beds with teachers, while its principal once wandered through a common area naked, former students claim.
A NSW parliamentary inquiry on Monday was told of the disturbing allegations from two former students of western Sydney’s Redeemer Baptist School.
Edward Garth, 23, said he was shunned after “escaping” the broader Redeemer community in November.
He told the committee about a study-stay during school holidays when he slept in the same building as principal and church elder Jonathon Cannon.
“I remember one night before dinner, I was in the kitchen getting a drink,” Garth said.
“As I walked into the living room, which was my bedroom at the time, I saw [Cannon], my principal, walk out of the bathroom into the living room naked before heading to his room.
“He was startled, and when they saw me, he ran to his room. I don’t know why he didn’t cover himself with a towel.”
Garth said he reported the incident, but it got back to Cannon, the principal’s brother Noel and the then-pupil’s own parents, who scolded him.
Former student Emma Hughes told the inquiry the culture inside the school left much for students to “untangle” as adults.
School camps, away from parents, were especially anxiety-inducing.
On occasion, a student would have to share a bed with teachers in a caravan park or school-owned cabins to save space, she said.
Her submission stated nothing untoward happened to her during the stays.
“Usually, the student would be a community member, which in itself says they knew maybe they shouldn’t be doing it,” she said.
“But I recall when I was in year 6, I would share a bed with [a] teacher, and in an effort to be fair, she made it so we would rotate every night … so that we all didn’t have to.”
Staff, often known by kinship titles like “uncle”, regularly crossed conversational boundaries, Hughes said.
“Often, personal things were discussed in very public matters,” she said.
after newsletter promotion
“The nature of boundaries is really something which is not particularly, I believe, understood by staff at Redeemer in the way we understand it in most school contexts.”
The school also had an emphasis on surveillance and “dobbing”, public humiliations and punishment, she said.
A boy and girl were made to stand on chairs in front of a year 7 class after teachers intercepted a love note, Hughes said of her time at the school.
Noel Cannon read the note to a collection of students before they were “dressed-down in front of four year groups and many teachers”, she said.
The parliamentary committee is investigating the management of the Parramatta-based school and oversight from government bodies.

The Communities and Justice Department received 15 risks of significant harm notifications since 2004 but they had not triggered a field assessment, an earlier response to questions on notice revealed.
Cannon and other school representatives were invited to appear at the inquiry and state the school’s case.
Committee chair Abigail Boyd said she was disappointed an attempted summons to appear went begging.
AAP has contacted the school for comment on the students’ allegations.

articles.title: Hurricane Simon batters Mexico's Pacific Coast
articles.summary: Hurricane Simon is currently running parallel to Mexico's Pacific Coast, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds to vulnerable towns.

image.caption: Authorities have established emergency shelters for those affected by the hurricaneImage: Daniel Becerril/REUTERS

blocks.text: Hurricane Simon lashed vulnerable resorts and towns along Mexico's Pacific Coast on Sunday as it moved parallel to the shoreline, despite weakening to a category 3 storm.
"Additional weakening is forecast but Simon is still expected to be a strong hurricane as it passes near the coast of west-central Mexico tonight," the US National Hurricane Center's advisory said.
Simon is expected to move farther offshore on Monday before turning back towards Mexico's coast on Wednesday, it said.
On high alert

Mexican authorities have placed 28 municipalities across the states of Jalisco and Colima under the highest cyclone alert level. Another 93 municipalities were under high ‌alert, according to civil protection bulletins.

blocks.caption: Strong winds are battering the coastal states on the Pacific end of MexicoImage: Daniel Becerril/REUTERS

blocks.text: The hurricane's center closed in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rains were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Puerto Vallarta is a popular tourist destination in Jalisco. Apart from the resorts, several Mexicans live in communities inland and uphill, in houses that may not be able to weather the storm.
How to protect houses from natural disasters
Experts believe the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.

"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin said.

"They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."

blocks.caption: heavy rainfall overnight has increased the risk of flooding and muslidesImage: Daniel Becerril/REUTERS

blocks.text: In Manzanillo, residents waded through flooded streets on Sunday morning as soldiers helped rescue locals from the overnight rainfall.
"The beds, the refrigerators, the stoves, all the furniture got wet. The whole house flooded," Cecilia Palomar told Reuters outside her home.
How do tropical storms form?
"My mother doesn't want ‌to leave. We took her to my brother's, to higher ground. She's an elderly woman, but ‌she doesn't ​want to leave. She doesn't want to be away from her home."
Airport closed, authorities urge caution
Puerto Vallarta International Airport was closed temporarily while authorities suspended non-essential activities.
They also established emergency shelters in threatened coastal communities.
Earlier on Sunday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum had urged residents of coastal communities in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain indoors ahead of the storm.
Hurricane Simon has come days after Hurricane Polo struck Mexico's Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 storm, knocking down power lines and flooding the streets.

articles.title: Indian opposition leaders march to top court to demand election chief resign
articles.summary: The march follows a chaotic weekend in Delhi which saw thousands of protesters being detained by police.

blocks.text: India's opposition parties are marching to the Supreme Court in Delhi to demand the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter fraud.
This will be the latest in a series of demonstrations in Delhi, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital.
Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janata Party pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained.

Opposition parties allege that under Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, India's voter rolls are being manipulated to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the charge.
The opposition lawmakers want to submit a memorandum to Chief Justice Surya Kant, but he has told reporters he declined the meeting citing "certain reasons".

He did not provide the reasons, but media reports citing the letter have said that he pointed out that some of the issues the opposition wanted to raise with him were also pending before the court. The BBC has not seen the letter.
"Every Indian citizen has the right to approach the court, and we will hear their concerns and grant whatever is due under the law," he told reporters.
Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, has called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march.

In a press conference on Monday, he shared a letter that he and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge had written to the Chief Justice, laying out their concerns with Kumar's alleged conduct and with the contentious electoral roll revision.
He said that Kant had asked them to file a petition, which they would do at the end of their march.

Authorities in Delhi have announced heavy restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some key metro stations. There is also heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march.

Several thousand people were on Barakhamba road, where the march began, as a bus carrying Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders arrived just before 15:30 local time. Supporters waved flags and chanted his name as the Congress MP and others waved through the windows. Seated a few rows behind Rahul was Neha Bora, a leftist student leader who has gained prominence for participating in the protests.
Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi.
On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down.

The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened.

But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut down and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters.
The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the protest.

They were only released a day later - while Dipke has returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders, however, did not join the protests on Sunday but have said they will seek a new protest date from the police.

Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.
The BBC also captured visuals, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi Police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.
In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists.
"Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said.
Congress leader Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up.
BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were.

articles.title: Doctor warned Elizabeth Struhs would not be safe at home years before religious sect killed her by withdrawing medicine
articles.summary:
Coronial inquest begins into death of eight-year-old after 14 members of Toowoomba sect the Saints, including her parents, were found guilty of her manslaughter

  • Get our

blocks.text: A medical specialist at the Queensland Children’s hospital warned that Elizabeth Struhs would not be safe at home with her mother years before her parents allowed her to die by withdrawing lifesaving medicine, a coronial inquest has heard.

Elizabeth, a type 1 diabetic, died at the age of eight from diabetic ketoacidosis on 7 January 2022, at her family home in Toowoomba, west of Brisbane, after her parents and other members of a religious sect withdrew the insulin she needed to survive and sat around singing and praying while she slowly died over the course of several days.

All 14 adult members of the sect, known as the Saints, were convicted of her manslaughter last year, including her father, Jason Struhs, mother, Kerrie Struhs, and brother, Zachary Struhs, and the leader of their sect, Brendan Stevens.
The group, which some have referred to as “a cult”, did not believe in medicine, and believed Elizabeth would be miraculously healed of her incurable illness and be resurrected after she died.

Elizabeth had been hospitalised in 2019 in a similar incident. Her mother, Kerrie, openly refused to provide her medical care and was charged and convicted with failing to provide her the necessaries of life as a result of the incident in 2021.
A coronial inquest, which sat for its first day on Monday, heard that doctors had attempted to warn the child safety department that Elizabeth could not be safely returned to Kerrie.

Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard heard from an experienced medical specialist who helped care for Elizabeth after her admission to the Queensland children’s hospital’s intensive care unit on 17 July 2019. The doctor cannot be identified for legal reasons.
The doctor wrote a professional report about the child one day later raising concerns about her safety, the inquest heard.
The doctor said she was concerned partly due to Elizabeth’s condition at presentation, describing her as “extremely unwell” and requiring intubation and a ventilator.
But she was also concerned about the religious beliefs of Elizabeth’s mother, Kerrie, she said.
Kerrie refused to even attend the hospital to see her child, and denied that she was sick or would ever require medication in a phone conversation, the doctor told the court.
Kerrie also had no questions about her daughter’s condition, the doctor said.
Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris read from the doctor’s nine-page report, which was sent to child safety and the police.
“‘Type 1 diabetes is a life-threatening condition that requires complicated care by the parents, the report reads,” he said.
“If her mother continues to deny the requirement for insulin and the related treatments Elizabeth could not be in Kerrie’s care’.
“With ‘not’ in bold,” Hamlyn-Harris added.
The doctor consulted the hospital’s child protection and forensic medical service before writing the report.
after newsletter promotion
“My concerns were so strong that if [a nurse at the service] had said not to I was still planning to submit a report,” the doctor said.

Elizabeth was ultimately returned home to live with her family, with an intervention parental agreement: a short-term, voluntary, intensive arrangement which allows child safety authorities to aid a child in danger without a child protection order, the inquest heard.
The court heard this was done without the knowledge of the hospital team.
“There is still significant risk in that context,” the doctor said, on Monday.
“I would not be supportive of that treatment if I was the clinician involved in that discharge home plan.”
The doctor said she raised concerns at the time that diabetes required lifelong treatment, and that the risk posed by the illness can change over time, due to physical or social changes.
Elizabeth’s father, Jason, agreed to care for Elizabeth after her discharge from hospital, which he did for three years.

At the time, Jason was a longtime sceptic of his wife’s religion, and had saved Elizabeth’s life by taking her to hospital against the wishes of his wife in 2019 and then testified against her at a criminal trial.

Both Jason and Kerrie were found guilty in 2021 of failing to supply the necessaries of life for their daughter, relating to the incident in 2019 which was so serious Elizabeth was taken to hospital in a coma.

Jason was sentenced to six months in prison, wholly suspended for a period of 12 months, while Kerrie was sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment with a specified parole release date of 15 December 2021.
But Kerrie helped convert Jason to her religious beliefs while serving her prison sentence. He was then convinced to give up treating Elizabeth’s diabetes with insulin, leading to her death.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: Mystery of 1950s wedding photo album found dumped in Wakefield solved
articles.summary:
Online appeal and detective work by local historian help to return keepsake to couple’s sone after it had been stolen

When Andrew Bedford discovered an old wedding album…

blocks.text: When Andrew Bedford discovered an old wedding album dumped outside his city centre cafe in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, he considered chucking it into a nearby wheelie bin.
But when he opened the album, the vintage photographs of the happy couple on their wedding day in 1957 seemed too precious to throw away.
Unable to work out the identity of the bride and groom – their handwritten names had become too faded to read – he rescued the album and brought it back to his cafe, Eva’s Kitchen, for safekeeping.
His partner, Éva Lemperger, put out a plea on social media to help identify the couple.
Now the mystery has been solved after a local family historian took up the case and tracked down the couple’s 65-year-old son, Michael Dawson.
He revealed the album had been stolen from a storage unit near the cafe, along with other cherished family heirlooms, after his parents died.
It contains some of his only surviving photographs of his mother and father, Maxwell Dawson and Barbara Parr, and he now plans to “protect it with [his] life”.

blocks.caption: The wedding photos were found to be of Maxwell Dawson and Barbara Parr. Photograph: Andrew Bedford

blocks.text: Bedford said: “I was just so happy he got it back. I thought, if it had been mine, and I’d lost pictures of my family – and they were only pictures I had of them – I’d have been elated if somebody had found them and given them back to me.”

When the case of the mysterious wedding album was picked up by his local newspaper, the Wakefield Express, it caught the attention of a local historian and amateur sleuth, Anne-Marie Fawcett. “I run a local history group on Facebook with over 15,000 members, and I’m really interested in local history, particularly family history,” she said.

“I love researching. I love uncovering stories and finding connections. And I like getting to the bottom of mysteries … When I saw that nobody knew who the album belonged to, I thought, that’s something to get my teeth into.”

A clue in the birth certificate of another guest helped her to identify the church the couple were married in: Wadsley Parish Church in Sheffield. She then used a photo enhancing tool to decipher the name of the bride. “But there was more than one Barbara Parr in the records, so I had to follow them all.”

When she came across an electoral roll entry suggesting Parr’s husband, Maxwell, had lived near Wakefield, she guessed she had found the right couple and appealed for information about the family on social media.

blocks.caption: Eva’s Kitchen cafe in Wakefield, West Yorkshire. Photograph: Andrew Bedford

blocks.text: An old school friend of Michael Dawson’s remembered him and helped Fawcett to find a photograph of him, enabling her to track him down on Facebook.
“I sent him a message, and he rang me,” said Fawcett. “He was absolutely made up.”

Dawson told her the album had been stolen from the storage unit where he and his brother had stored the cherished contents of his parents’ home after they died. “Someone had broken in and taken all the family treasure. He said he’d lost everything. So you can imagine how I felt to be able to reunite him with this [album] … I’ve got goose pimples talking about it. Everybody loves a happy ending, don’t they?”
Dawson told the BBC: “I’m absolutely elated because I am sentimental and it’s important for me to have these photos.
“I will protect it with my life now, based on the fact that it’s all I’ve got.”
Asked how he felt about Fawcett’s detective efforts, he joked: “I think she probably knows more about me than I do, which is a worry.”
But he added: “I thought I’d lost everything. I can’t thank her enough.”

articles.title: UK van drivers face extra £2.5bn in diesel costs this year, figures show
articles.summary:
Calls for planned fuel duty rise to be scrapped as analysis finds average fuel bill could hit £1,965, up from £1,294

Millions of British van drivers face a combined £2.5bn cost to cover the…

blocks.text: Millions of British van drivers face a combined £2.5bn cost to cover the rising price of diesel this year, according to figures, fuelling calls for the government to scrap its planned fuel duty rise.

The owners of diesel vans and pickups can expect to collectively spend almost £8.5bn at the pump this year, according to analysis for the Guardian, after diesel prices climbed to record highs due to a global fuel shortage caused by disruption to refineries in the Middle East and Russia.

The estimated fuel costs, calculated by analysts at Moneysupermarket, is significantly above the £5.95bn spent last year, raising concerns that the price of food and goods transported by road could rise sharply as retailers pass on increased logistics costs.

The comparison site warned last week that the average fuel bill for a van driver could reach £1,965 this year, up from £1,294 for the average van in 2025 based on typical mileage and fuel consumption.
The number of vans on British roads has grown significantly in recent years fuelled by the boom in online shopping, home deliveries and the rising number of self-employed people working in trades.

Although the adoption of electric vans has begun to increase, about 95% of light commercial vehicles are still powered by diesel. The average pump price climbed to a above £2 a litre for the first time this month, up over 40% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy.

The rising cost burden has led to calls for government help in the upcoming budget, including abandoning plans to raise fuel duty from next year. The planned increase – postponed from September – will add 3p a litre in duty from 1 January, and another 2p from 1 March, in “a hammer blow” for costs, according to the Road Haulage Association (RHA).

Richard Smith, the RHA’s managing director, said: “Many of our members run on margins of around 2%. Surging diesel prices are impacting firms across the country, with some spending many thousands extra every week on fuel.
“Adding [fuel duty rises] on top of today’s fuel prices would be a hammer blow for many firms that move goods and the households that buy them. A fuel duty hike is a food price hike.”

Data from the motoring group RAC showed that, despite a recent dip in the cost of diesel, the price remains about 57p a litre higher than before the US-Iran conflict while petrol remains 42p higher. This means households are paying £31 and £23 more respectively every time they fill up a family sized car, according to the group.
The fuel duty rise “will only make prices at the pump even more expensive,” according to Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC.

“As things stand, this year is still set to be the second most expensive year on record for drivers,” Williams said. “The government has the power to take some of the sting out of higher fuel costs, either by extending and increasing the fuel duty cut or reducing VAT as they’ve done with domestic electricity.”

Smith added that the RHA was calling on the chancellor to bring in a 15p a litre rebate for British van, coach and haulage operators after Spain, France and Italy offered similar help for commercial vehicle businesses. “It’s time we caught up,” he said.

On Friday, the US president, Donald Trump, attempted to ease pressure at the pump for US drivers by announcing a deal for Russian deal, in a move which infuriated the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The government was contact for comment.

articles.title: Delhi police shut metro stations ahead of election protest march
articles.summary:
India’s opposition parties and supporters of the ‘cockroach’ youth movement have been demonstrating against a ⁠controversial revision of election voter ⁠lists

Authorities in India’s capital…

blocks.text: Authorities in India’s capital closed six metro stations and warned of traffic disruptions on Monday, as opposition parties planned to march to the supreme court in protest against a ⁠controversial revision of voter ⁠lists that has sparked days ​of unrest in Delhi.

Opposition parties and supporters of the “cockroach” youth movement have taken to the streets almost daily this month to demand the resignation of chief election commissioner ⁠Gyanesh Kumar over the revision that critics say benefits prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).

The revision that started last year saw over 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – deleted from voter lists during a verification exercise, including 30 million who could not be traced. Others included 28 million people who had died, and 63 million who had relocated.

Opposition parties allege Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions – charges both the poll panel and BJP reject.

Police detained thousands of protesters in Delhi over the weekend, including leaders ​of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), as supporters of the youth movement ‌sought to march in protest and were ‌stopped by thousands of security personnel who locked down central Delhi.

The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted ‌voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.

blocks.caption: Security personnel detain demonstrators during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner on Sunday. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Police said the six metro stations were closed on Monday for “security reasons” and traffic restrictions and diversions would be imposed in 20 locations.
The main opposition Congress party has announced a march to the supreme court to submit a memorandum to the Chief Justice demanding an end to what it calls “vote theft” and Kumar’s resignation.
“Youth, all opposition parties, civil society groups, all those who believe in democracy and stand by the ‌Constitution of India, will walk with us,” Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said on X.

Chief Justice Surya Kant, however, declined a meeting request in an email, saying Gandhi and the ​Congress delegation should instead approach the court legally since the issue was already being heard by the court and should be addressed through judicial proceedings, a Congress source said.
Separately, the CJP said its leaders would meet Delhi police to “demand” a date for a peaceful protest. It has threatened to announce a new call to protest if a date is not given within 24 hours.

The youth movement, which has mobilised protests in recent months ⁠against issues ranging from government school infrastructure to jobs, is one of the biggest political challenges to ​Modi and his BJP in his 12 ​years in power.

The protests erupted after the ​Indian Express newspaper reported last month that Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, ​registration procedures and digital systems.
