articles.title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth
articles.summary: Backdated paperwork also made the Russian oligarch’s yachts and mansions disappear from accounts, BBC finds.
articles.byline: James Oliver, Rory Tinman, Simon Lock

blocks.text: The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.
Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.
Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".

Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".
The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.

For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.

Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.
The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".
Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.

Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.
Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.
This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.
It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.
But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.

An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.
MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.
A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree".
MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.
This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.

Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.
So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.

Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.

Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."

In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.
MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.
It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.

Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.

MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.
Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear.

articles.title: Burnham to urge MPs to embrace closer ties with EU
articles.summary:
Post-recess statement will focus on damage caused by Brexit and the need to cooperate on immigration and trade

Andy Burnham will put Brexit back on the Commons agenda as MPs return from…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham will put Brexit back on the Commons agenda as MPs return from recess, warning that failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty”.

The prime minister will use a statement to the Commons on the first day back after the party conference break to urge MPs to face up to the damage caused by Brexit, and embrace closer ties with the EU to increase economic growth and tackle illegal immigration.

In a stern warning ahead of the upcoming UK-EU summit, Burnham will argue that Britain cannot afford to turn its back on opportunities for greater cooperation with Europe and that maintaining the status quo is no longer good enough.
He will call for a calm, clear-eyed assessment of Britain’s relationship with Europe and urge MPs from across the Commons to back a pragmatic approach.
Burnham is expected to argue that most of the public would expect the government to seize the opportunity if closer cooperation could strengthen immigration controls while reviving the economy.

A No 10 source said: “Andy understands why some politicians don’t want to face up to the reality that Brexit has not delivered what they once promised. But it is time for a different conversation about what our long-term relationship should be.
“Sticking with the status quo and not working relentlessly to secure a good deal that boosts growth would be a major dereliction of duty.”
The prime minister’s statement comes on the same day MPs are due to debate a petition in Westminster Hall, calling for Britain to apply to rejoin the EU, which got more than 111,000 signatures.

The intervention comes amid renewed divisions over Britain’s relationship with Europe, with senior Conservatives vowing to reverse Labour’s moves towards closer EU ties, including a proposed agreement designed to ease post-Brexit barriers on food and agricultural trade. It has prompted warnings from businesses that abandoning such arrangements could prolong costs and uncertainty caused by checks and paperwork at the border.

But the idea of Britain having a closer relationship with the EU has also prompted unease within Burnham’s own ranks. Some MPs representing leave-voting constituencies fear renewing the Brexit debate could reopen old divisions, with senior ministers warning of the political and economic risks of pursuing EU membership.

Burnham’s statement also follows his declaration on Sunday that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum. The prime minister has said he sought clarification on foreign interference after entering Downing Street and received confirmation of Russian involvement, although he did not reveal the evidence or suggest it had changed the referendum result.
after newsletter promotion
The prime minister has already signalled a significant change in tone from his predecessor Keir Starmer, who ruled out rejoining the single market or customs union.

At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done more harm than good and promised to examine Britain’s longterm relationship with the EU. He opened the door to options including fully rejoining the bloc.

Monday’s statement will turn the focus towards the immediate negotiations, with ministers seeking progress on removing trade barriers, including bureaucracy affecting food imports and exports, and closer cooperation on migration.

articles.title: How Iran's elite forces 'mold the minds of the young cadets'
articles.summary: Months of correspondence with two high-ranking defectors have given DW's investigative unit a rare look at the mindset of the regime's loyal servants — and revealed a clandestine circle that…

image.caption: The two men gave DW insight into the workings of Iran's security forcesImage: DW

blocks.text: Omid, whose real name cannot be used, signed up to join Iran's security forces when he was 18 years old and harbored "a deep commitment to my country." At the academy, Omid told DW, cadets were under the regime's control "day and night," from their military training through the daily prayers and speeches.
"They mold the minds of the young cadets," Omid said.

Some of these recruits, Omid said, eventually rise through the ranks of Iran's security apparatus to join an elite cadre of officers who plot missions, abductions and assassinations inside and outside of Iran — and have access to unlimited resources and personnel. And, he said, he attended their meetings.

blocks.caption: "Omid" was a commander in Iran's special forces. Image: DW

blocks.text: A defector speaks

When Omid, a burly man who carries scars accumulated during his decades-long service as a commander with Iran's elite special forces, reached out in early 2026, deliberations ensued: Could he have been sent to feed DW misinformation and lies to discredit the broadcaster, whose Farsi service is officially sanctioned in Iran? Could he be trying to harm DW or its Iranian employees?

Over the course of months, journalists from DW's investigative unit and Persian department corresponded with him. Omid shared records and photos of his training, which ranged from sniper practice and surveillance to street fighting, riot control and parachuting courses. He also provided photos and videos, documents and locations of a secret monitoring center and housing compounds reserved for high-ranking members of the Iranian security forces.
United in their absolute loyalty to Iran's supreme leader, he said, a clandestine circle of high-ranking officers plot and execute the murder and abductions of the regime's opponents.

Omid's testimony offered a rare insight into Iran's powerful and opaque security apparatus — and into the lives of the men at the core of the Islamic Republic — allowing DW to piece together a picture of how the regime has maintained deeply loyal forces despite widespread protest movements, international sanctions, rising inflation and recent attacks by its two main enemies, Israel and the United States, that eliminated much of its top military and political leadership.

DW corroborated substantial parts of Omid's account with documents, photos, videos and interviews with experts. An intermediary connected the investigative team with a second high-ranking defector, whose account corroborated key details provided by Omid. Though DW confirmed both men's identities, we are withholding certain details to protect them and their families.

blocks.caption: "Omid" and "Reza" provided images and documentsImage: Privat

blocks.text: In the past, Iran has gone after dissidents and opposition activists abroad, including journalists.
We asked the Embassy or Iran in Berlin and the Supreme Leader’s Office to respond to our findings. The Supreme Leader's Office did not reply.
The embassy in Berlin declined to address the individual allegations, stating that "the Islamic Republic of Iran firmly rejects these allegations and the conclusions drawn from them."
Prayers and privileges

As a high-ranking member of the special forces, Omid had access to the privileges the regime often bestows upon its own: From financial incentives and lucrative economic contracts for their own enterprises to special housing compounds, with their own mosques, schools and hospitals, where personal satellite dishes are banned and religious observance is enforced.

blocks.caption: Omid's training included parachuting courses. Image: Privat

blocks.text: These privileges have their price, Omid said: "control, nothing but control." Officers are tightly monitored. "You're not allowed to just attend a wedding or travel," he said. "They confiscate your passport; they even decide which schools your children are allowed to attend."

The control extends to soldiers' prospective partners, who are first vetted by the regime. Even then, Omid said, he was not allowed to share the true nature of his work with his wife. That, he said, "really eats away at you."

By separating such agents from regular Iranians, the regime can keep a closer eye on its forces, said Saeid Golkar, political scientist at the University of Tennessee, who has extensively researched the command structure of the Islamic Republic's security apparatus. "They can create peer pressure and indoctrinate much more effectively," Golkar told DW.
And, Golkar said, security forces who are largely segregated from regular Iranians are less likely to balk at using force against their civilian compatriots.
A defector from Iran's intelligence agency

A month into DW's interactions with Omid, an intermediary connected us with another high-ranking defector. The man, whom we're calling Reza, worked with the Information Ministry, Iran's intelligence agency.

Like many who are recruited into the security apparatus, Reza hails from a religious family: He grinned as he showed DW a picture on his phone of himself as a young man, sporting the long beard and turban favored by the devout in Iran.

blocks.caption: "Reza" used to be an ardent supporter of the Iranian regime. Image: DW

blocks.text: Many of his relatives, he said, still occupy prominent positions in the Iranian regime.

In the early days, he was an ardent supporter of the regime and would sometimes cry during prayers, he said, knowing that he was serving his people and the Islamic Republic and "might even die as a martyr for Islam."

Reza said he slowly turned against the regime as he witnessed the clampdown on protesters. Over the years, officers have shot, arrested and beaten Iranians protesting the country's deteriorating living conditions and strict "morality" laws.
Nowadays, his hair is cropped short.
'Years serving a cruel system'

On the evening of January 8, amid an almost total internet shutdown, security forces opened fire on Iranians protesting widespread shortages and spiking inflation. The extent of the massacre slowly came to light as images trickled out of the country documenting the regime's atrocities.

blocks.caption: In January 2026, protesters took to the streets again. Image: UGC/DW

blocks.text: Thousands of protesters were killed across Iran. Both Omid and Reza said the mass killings which, human rights organizations report, included the shooting of unarmed protesters in hospital beds — had horrified them.
Indeed, this ongoing brutality ultimately led them to speak with DW.
Omid was adamant that he had never shot at protesters nor ordered his subordinates to do so, although DW is unable to corroborate this.
When pressed, he conceded that he had witnessed the killing of demonstrators.

Reza said the guilt he carried after having "wasted 10, 11 years serving a cruel system" compelled him to speak out despite the risk to him and his family. "The truth is: When your opponent is a regime that doesn't adhere to any moral values, you need to be prepared for anything," he said.
Who are Iran's Revolutionary Guards?
Surveillance and suppression

Omid and Reza discussed secret command centers that are central to clamping down on protests. High-ranking members of all units and agencies gather in a monitoring room where, Omid and Reza say, huge monitors on the walls display real-time feeds from countless CCTV cameras around the capital, Tehran. They say there are other such rooms around the country.

Protest marches are also monitored from above by drones. And, Reza said, "information from forces on the ground and from Twitter, Telegram and other social networks, as well as information obtained through surveillance and interception devices — all this information is collected there."
Plainclothes agents often infiltrate protest groups. Omid said such agents were sometimes used to redirect protest marches to places where security forces lie in wait.
A representative of Iran's supreme leader "had a free hand" in ordering operations from within the command center, Omid said, as well as deciding "how harshly the protesters should be dealt with."

When regular police can no longer quell demonstrations, Omid and Reza said, elite units from the Revolutionary Guard and police, often clad entirely in black, their faces hidden behind balaclavas, are sent in to finish the job.

blocks.caption: Documents DW obtained reveal the design of forces deployed to quell protestsImage: DW

blocks.text: Human rights organizations have documented the use of automatic and semiautomatic machine guns and even heavy machine guns mounted on top of pickup trucks to clamp down on protests.

"The fact that the security forces are equipped with military-grade firearms that were designed for combat situations, for responding to protests, shows that the killings of protesters in the country are intended," finds Amnesty International Iran researcher Raha Bahreini, the author of a recent report analyzing the regime's chain of command during the 2022 protests following the death of Jina Mahsa Aminiin custody.
The Dakhme 'killing machine'

After months of correspondence, Omid pointed DW to an outwardly unremarkable location in Shahr-e Rey, on the outskirts of Tehran: A prayer hall sandwiched between an occupational therapy practice and a pharmacy. Though the prayer hall is named Beit al Shohada, or the house of martyrs, Omid said many officers call the place Dakhme, meaning crypt or tomb.

blocks.caption: The men allegedly meet in this prayer hall on Pilgush StreetImage: Privat

blocks.text: Omid described how high-ranking officers met under Dakhme's corrugated iron roof to plot off-the-books operations that bypass government structures. He said he had attended several meetings at Dakhme "where decisions about murder are made: It's a killing machine."

Though Omid insisted repeatedly that he had only attended the meetings because he had been ordered to by his higher-ups and he had never taken part in any of the operations plotted at Dakhme, he listed murders and abductions within and outside of Iran that he said were planned there. DW could not verify these cases but found that some of the people named had indeed died under unresolved circumstances.

Several experts DW contacted knew of Dakhme in connection with a murder attempt on an adviser to a reformist president over two decades ago. Others had never heard of Dakhme. No one DW spoke with could confirm its continued operation.

Experts agree that a facility such as Dakhme is plausible. "The Islamic Republic probably feels more of a need now to have these types of groups," Miad Maleki, a former US Treasury official who until recently designed US sanctions programs targeting Iran, told DW.
Indeed, Maleki said, military operations planned covertly at Dakhme would likely give the regime plausible deniability in cases of killings.

blocks.caption: DW obtained rare images of a religious gathering inside Dakhme.

blocks.text: Religious and ruthless

Because of the secrecy surrounding Dakhme, much of the following is based only on Omid's accounts and the rare images DW obtained of religious ceremonies inside the hall. The secret meetings usually kick off under the guise of religious ceremonies and rituals, he said, in a large hall often adorned with green drapes and religious banners. After a communal dinner, only those in the inner circle stay.

Those who remain hand over their mobile phones, which are locked away. Then, Omid said, "seasoned specialists from Iran's special forces and intelligence operation " discuss murder and abductions late into the night.

"For these people, a person's position isn't that important," Omid said. "If they consider someone a threat to the supreme leader of the Islamic Republic, they take it extremely seriously and take action."
After each operation, Omid said, the men return to their respective roles within Iran's security apparatus, until they gather again to defend the Islamic Republic at any cost.
Additional research by: Youhanna Najdi
Translation from Farsi by: Farhad Payar
Copyedited by: Milan Gagnon
Fact-checked by: Carolyn Thompson
Legal advice: Florian Wagenknecht

articles.title: Marcos touts business, energy investments after Singapore visit
articles.summary: Marcos highlights investment deals with Singapore-based firms.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 12:58pm
This screenshot photo shows President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivering an arrival statement upon his return to the Philippines on October 12, 2026 after a five-day working visit in Singapore.
RTVM / Philstar.com's screenshot
MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. highlighted the investment commitments from Singapore-based firms upon his arrival in the Philippines after a five-day working visit.
Marcos arrived back in the country at around 1:54 a.m. on Monday, October 12, The STAR reported.

In his arrival statement, Marcos said he met with executives of FedEx, Mitsubishi Corp. and Vena Energy during his visit to Singapore, where investment pledges for the Philippine business and energy sectors were discussed.
Business investments

According to Marcos, Mitsubishi’s $700 million investment in Ayala Corp. was a significant deal, as it is “expected to be among the largest foreign equity investments in the Philippines in recent years.”
The recent deal would reportedly increase Mitsubishi’s ownership stake in Ayala Corp. from 4.7% to 15%.
Meanwhile, Marcos said FedEx had expressed strong interest in expanding its Clark Gateway Hub in Pampanga, which is expected to open in the last quarter of 2028.

This expansion, the president added, is set to help small and medium enterprises, or MSMEs, sell their products in the international market through the facility’s increased capacity to handle more air cargo and specialized shipments.
Renewable energy expansion
For the energy sector, Vena Energy had expressed its intention to expand its presence in the Philippines, which Marcos said is in line with the country’s energy agenda.

The president said the firm is planning to build more facilities that generate electricity from renewable sources to add generating capacity to its existing operations and produce up to 1.29 gigawatts of power.
Vena Energy is planning to invest P52 billion in this expansion project over the next two years, Marcos added.
The company’s existing operations in the Philippines include operational facilities with a combined capacity of 887 megawatts and other projects under construction with a capacity of 1.26 gigawatts.
Marcos said the investment pledge is aligned with the government’s goal of achieving a 35% renewable energy share in the country’s power supply by 2030 and 50% by 2040.

“I am confident that the interest shown by investors in these engagements will bring more high value investments, partnerships, technology, and jobs to the Philippines, particularly in sectors that will support our long-term growth and transformation,” Marcos said.
Nuclear energy plans. Meanwhile, Marcos said he also visited the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute to learn from the country’s studies on nuclear energy as a power source.
Marcos has consistently expressed support for integrating nuclear energy into the country’s power mix to lower electricity costs.
His push for nuclear energy has drawn criticism and concerns, especially from environmental advocates, over safety, radioactive waste management and financial risks.

articles.title: Remulla to Supreme Court: Time to review anti-plunder law amid flood control scandal
articles.summary: In his first year at the Office of the Ombudsman, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has urged the Supreme Court to revisit the anti-plunder law.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 12:19pm

Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla speaks to reporters after taking his oath before Supreme Court Associate Justice Marvic Leonen as the new Ombudsman during a ceremony at the Supreme Court in Manila on Wednesday, Oct. 9, 2025.
The STAR / Edd Gumban
MANILA, Philippines — In his first year at the Office of the Ombudsman, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has urged the Supreme Court to revisit the anti-plunder law.
In his speech on Monday, October 12, Remulla said that securing convictions faces a major legal hurdle: the 2016 Supreme Court ruling in Macapagal-Arroyo v. People.
“Kaya sinasabi ko ito nang may buong paggalang sa Kataas-taasang Hukuman: panahon na para balikan ang doktrinang ito. It is time to revisit it,” Remulla said in his speech.
(That is why I say this with all due respect to the Supreme Court: it is time to revisit this doctrine. It is time to revisit it.)

The doctrine, according to Remulla, introduced two requirements not originally written by Congress into the plunder law: first, that the prosecution must identify a "main plunderer"; and second, that it must prove the accused personally received or benefited from the stolen funds.
“Think about what that means. The smarter the thief, the safer he is. Pass the money through enough dummies, middlemen and shell companies, and no one can be shown to have touched it,” Remulla said.
He argued that while the plunder law was designed to hold those who steal billions accountable, the current doctrine makes the largest syndicates the hardest to catch.
“Hindi po iyan hustisya. Pananggalang po iyan,” he said.
(That is not justice. That is a shield.)
Remulla added that the ongoing flood control cases mirror the complex, multi-layered schemes protected by the current plunder doctrine.
“Let us not forget the size and magnitude of this scandal. Over a hundred billion pesos was paid for flood control projects that were never built,” Remulla said.
“Hindi substandard. Hindi kulang. Wala talaga,” he added.
(Not substandard. Not lacking. There is nothing at all.)
Philstar.com has reached out to the Supreme Court for comment on Remulla’s pronouncement, but it has yet to reply.

articles.title: US judge orders halt to taxpayer-funded promo ads of Trump
articles.summary: Last week, President Donald Trump said he considered the ads to be a "positive promotion for our great USA."

image.caption: Trump said he considered the ads to be 'rather standard'Image: Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television ads paid for with millions in taxpayer money for political promotions, a federal court judge ruled on Sunday night, granting a temporary restraining order.
This comes after publicly funded television ads glorifying Trump began airing in late September, sparking bipartisan backlash.
The commercials feature Trump promoting his policies and warning against communism and of a "final battle" against "globalists."
They end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government.
What did the judge say?
New York District Judge Jennifer L Rochon called the commercials an illegal misuse of funds, siding with a coalition which includes the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause.

"Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements" during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.

The court ordered the halt even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end. In a court filing late on Saturday, the Justice Department had argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because "the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow."
What is the controversy?
The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million (€17.8 million) taxpayer funds to run the ads in question.
Legal experts argue that it violates a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda," along with other laws potentially.
On Monday, Trump had said he considered the ads to be "rather standard" and a "positive promotion for our great USA," but that they would not be funded by taxpayers any longer.
The White House said last week that the president's political action committee would fund the ads going forward but not reimburse taxpayers for the ones that had already run on their dime.
Trump proclaims US 'golden age' of science

"There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda," the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, a nonprofit organization that represents them.

"We won't stop until this administration is ‌held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste ‌and ​abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again," said Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomon.

The plaintiffs, which included a public employee union and a candidate for Alabama state representative, urged the judge to block the ads by Friday so they would not air during weekend programming, such as football games and Saturday Night Live.
US Democrats have also challeneged the ads in a seperate suit filed at a federal court in Washington.

articles.title: Robert Pether was detained in Iraq in 2021 and his family feared he would die in jail. Now he’s coming home
articles.summary: Australian foreign minister welcomes Iraqi government’s decision to allow engineer to leave Baghdad

blocks.text: Australian engineer Robert Pether has been allowed to leave Iraq after a four-year stint in a Baghdad jail cell that his family feared would kill him.

Pether’s family say they have been “living in hell” since he was arrested without charge in April 2021 in connection to a business dispute between his firm – which was building a new headquarters for the central bank – and the Iraqi government.
He was imprisoned for more than four years but then released mid-last year due to his deteriorating health. He was banned from leaving the country.
The Australian foreign minister, Penny Wong, confirmed on Monday that Pether had now been allowed to leave the country. It was understood he was in transit.
“The Australian government welcomes the Iraqi government’s decision to allow Mr Robert Pether to leave Iraq today,” Wong said.
“I spoke to Mr Pether shortly before his departure from Baghdad and am pleased he is now free to move forward with his life and be reunited with his family.”
“Today’s outcome follows many years of persistent advocacy by the Australian government, including at the highest levels of government, and sustained consular assistance to Mr Pether and his family.”

Pether and his colleague Khalid Radwan were detained in Baghdad in April 2021 after flying in for a meeting with bank officials to resolve a dispute they were having with his engineering firm, CME Consulting.
Pether was later sentenced and fined over allegations that his firm spent money that should have gone to an architect and a subcontractor.
In a report in March 2022, the United Nations working group on arbitrary detention found Pether had been arbitrarily detained in breach of international law.

The UN body also found the arrest constituted an “enforced disappearance” and may have involved forms of torture. The working group said it had received complaints that Pether “was exposed to extreme cold, threats of death, humiliation and various forms of psychological abuse.”

“Mr Pether was detained in a [2x2 metre] cell with the lights permanently on,” the working group said in its report. “He was reportedly blindfolded, interrogated, screamed at, threatened, insulted and shown torture rooms.”
Pether’s family described the arrest and ongoing detention as a living nightmare.

It caused dramatic deterioration to Pether’s health. In 2022, the Guardian obtained an emotional letter from Pether to his family, penned from behind bars. The letter warned his family that his prognosis was “bleak” and that he was facing a potential “death sentence”.
after newsletter promotion
Pether also wrote of his daily torment about how he should break it to his children that he might not be coming home.

“How do you tell a little girl who loves unicorns and cats that her daddy will not be coming home? How do you tell your children that you are proud of them but will not be sharing the accolades (and pitfalls) of their lives with them?,” Pether wrote.
“And toughest of all, how do you tell your wife, who is very much the other half of you, that you will not be keeping the promise you made to grow old together?”

His wife, Desree, who resides in Ireland, had previously been critical of the efforts of Australian officials to secure his release, but the Australian government said it had raised the case with Iraqi authorities more than 200 times.
Following her husband’s release last year, Desree said she was “grateful to everyone who contributed to this happening”.
The UN working group also posed serious questions about the conduct of Pether’s trial.

The 2022 report aired allegations that Pether’s evidence was mistranslated to indicate guilt and said that even during the trial “Pether and Radwan did not have clarity around their charges”, with charges being dropped during the hearing and replaced with others.

“In the light of the above, the Working Group concludes that the violations of the right to a fair trial and due process are of such gravity as to give the deprivation of liberty of Messrs Pether and Radwan is arbitrary,” the report said.

articles.title: ERC orders Meralco to refund P2.64 billion to customers
articles.summary: The Energy Regulatory Commission directed Meralco to refund around P2.64 billion in excess charges to its consumers.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 10:37am
Linemen install new transformers on an electric post along United Nations Avenue in Manila on March 22, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) has directed the Manila Electric Company (Meralco) on Monday, October 12, to refund around P2.64 billion in excess charges to its consumers.
The refund is expected to reduce bills by an average of P0.1020 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) for at least six months, according to the ERC.
The refund rates, however, differ according to customer class:

items: Flat streetlights - P0.1764 per kWh
Residential and General Service A - P0.1733 per kWh
General Service B - P0.1147 per kWh
Government hospitals, metered streetlights, and charitable institutions - P0.0706 per kWh
General Power - P0.514 per kWh
Generator Wheeling - P0.0128 per kWh

blocks.text: Residential customers and small businesses will receive the “largest reduction in their monthly bills relative to their consumption,” the ERC said.
The order to refund comes after the agency found in its initial review, or “true-up,” that Meralco collected more in distribution charges than its approved rate from January to June this year.
The ERC-approved distribution rate was only P1.3522 per kWh, while Meralco charged P1.5537 per kWh, resulting in excess charges of P0.2015 per kWh, or P5.36 billion more than the approved rate.
The agency said Meralco had proposed refunding the excess charges over 12 months at a rate of P0.0487 per kWh, but the ERC shortened this period to give customers “faster relief.”

“When Meralco collects more than it is entitled to, the ERC will make sure it is returned, and that it is returned quickly. By shortening the refund period to six months, we are giving consumers faster relief at a time when electricity prices remain elevated,” ERC Chairperson Saturnino Juan said in the statement.
The refund will be reflected as a separate line item on customers’ electricity bills labeled “AWAT (Refund)/Collect.”
The ERC noted, however, that the amount is still subject to review and verification during its final evaluation scheduled for October 16 to 23.

articles.title: 4 Filipinos hurt in Riyadh airport attack, 3 in ICU
articles.summary: Three of the four Filipinos injured in an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, remain in intensive care units (ICUs), while the fourth is expected to be discharged,…

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 9:11am
Travellers through stanchion lines at the departure terminal of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on April 2, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines — Three of the four Filipinos injured in an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, remain in intensive care units (ICUs), while the fourth is expected to be discharged, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said Sunday, October 12.
The four Filipinos are recovering at different hospitals in Riyadh, according to the DMW.

"Batay sa ulat ni Labor Attache Dominador Salangga ng Migrant Workers Office (MWO)-Riyadh, tatlo ang kasalukuyang nasa ICU samantalang ang isa pa ay set for discharge from the hospital," the agency said in a statement posted on Facebook.
(Based on a report by Labor Attache Dominador Salangga of the Migrant Workers Office (MWO)-Riyadh, three are currently in the ICU while the other is set for discharge from the hospital.)

The DMW said its teams, along with the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) in Riyadh, are monitoring the condition of the injured Filipinos and providing the necessary assistance and support.
"Wala namang naiulat na Pilipinong nasawi kaugnay ng insidente," the agency said.
(No Filipino deaths have been reported in connection with the incident.)
The MWO is also coordinating with local authorities and hospitals to determine whether other Filipinos were affected by the attack and ensure they receive the necessary assistance.

The DMW advised overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) in Saudi Arabia to avoid areas that could be targeted in attacks, including military installations and oil refineries. Those at airports were also told to stay away from crowded areas.
OFWs were urged to follow announcements from the Philippine Embassy, consulates and MWO offices in Saudi Arabia, as well as the social media pages of Saudi government agencies.

Those scheduled to return to the Philippines were advised to contact their airlines before heading to the airport or check the email addresses they used to book their flights for updates. The agency also advised OFWs to ask their employers to regularly check their emails.
The DMW reminded Filipinos not to take photos or videos of attacks or post them on social media, warning that these activities are strictly prohibited in Saudi Arabia and may carry penalties.
Filipinos who need assistance may contact the following offices:
Riyadh/Central Region

MWO Jeddah: +966 56 981 9720; [email protected]

blocks.text: The attack on Saturday, October 10, killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300 others, according to Saudi civil aviation officials. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed the group for the strike, which a diplomatic source attributed to a missile fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
A fresh Houthi strike hit the Riyadh airport on Sunday, killing a Pakistani resident and injuring 11 others, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said, according to Agence France-Presse.

The fresh attack caused property damage, the extent of which was still being assessed. Authorities extended the airport's closure by 24 hours until 9 p.m. GMT on Monday, or 5 a.m. Tuesday in the Philippines.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Bookmark this page for Rappler's comprehensive coverage of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial at the Senate

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

articles.title: Judge orders Trump administration to end taxpayer-funded TV ads
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally at F&M Bank Arena in Clarksville, Tenn., on Saturday. (Seth Herald/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.
Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million US in taxpayer money for ads
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the non-partisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads and called them an illegal misuse of funds.
In granting a temporary restraining order, she told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night.

"Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements" during the two-week duration of her order, Rochon said.

The White House did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment on Sunday night. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because "the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow."

items: Trump administration faces 2 lawsuits for taxpayer-funded ads as midterms draw near
Why pro-Trump ads — paid for with public money — are airing on U.S. TV

blocks.text: The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million US in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested they ran afoul of a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda" and potentially other federal laws.
The Homeland Security money tapped for the ads comes from a $175-million package Congress gave to the department as part of Trump's immigration enforcement agenda.
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies.

But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren't aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs. One of the ads is a near replica of a 2024 ad that Trump ran during his presidential re-election campaign.
