articles.title: Imran Khan’s party decries ‘coup’ after Pakistan suspends provincial government
articles.summary:
Suspension of provincial government escalates standoff with Khan’s PTI party a week after his supporters began marching to demand his release

Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in a…

blocks.text: Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in a province ⁠led by Imran ​Khan’s PTI party and suspended its government, a move a party spokesperson described as “more of a coup disguised as emergency”.

President Asif Ali Zardari ​declared the emergency in the north-western Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Sunday, after the federal government said authorities there had failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province bordering Afghanistan.

The state of emergency and imposition of a new governor in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa sharply escalates a standoff between ⁠Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government, and comes a week after PTI supporters gathered in the province intending to march on Islamabad to demand Khan’s release.
Hundreds of activists and three of Khan’s sisters were detained before the planned march, in ​what the PTI called one of the strongest crackdowns in years.

Khan’s aide and PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari called the government’s move “more of a coup disguised as emergency,” adding that it risked inciting more bloodshed and instability and was intended to stop the protest.

Pakistan’s constitution ‌allows the government to take over from ‌provincial authorities during an emergency, and the law minister, Azam Nazeer Tarar, said a provincial governor would take charge in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number ‌of militant attacks in recent months.

Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad that the governor will initially be in place for six months, but could stay for as long as needed. The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the province.
The federal government and the military accuse PTI of failing to curb militants. The party rejects the charge and says Islamabad has not provided the funding and equipment it needs.
Restrictions have been placed on the movements of Sohail Afridi, who had previously been in charge of the province, one of his close aides told Reuters.

Maulana Fazlur Rehman, leader of the JUI-F political party and engaged by the government to mediate with PTI, also condemned the move. “Imposition of emergency is an ambush on democracy,” he told a news conference in Islamabad.
In Islamabad, the government has deployed tens of thousands of security forces and lined roads with containers ready to block roads, to bar protesters from reaching parliament.

Candidates backed by Khan’s party won the most seats ⁠in the 2024 election but formed a government only in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Supporters of the 74-year-old former cricket star say ​the military rigged the vote against him, which the ​military denies.

Cases against Khan range from concerns over state ​gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All but one conviction have been suspended or overturned, ​with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.
President Zardari ​declared the emergency on the advice of ​the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, after a cabinet decision, the president’s office said.
Sharif told the cabinet that security forces and citizens had been under attack for two years. “We can’t just act as a silent spectator.”
Islamabad also accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says PTI has sympathised with the Taliban in Kabul and its domestic affiliates. Both deny the charge.

articles.title: Watch: Endangered orangutans released back into the wild after Borneo fires
articles.summary: The critically endangered apes were rescued from intense wildfires that destroyed their habitat in August and September.

blocks.text: Eight orangutans have been released into the wild in Borneo after being rescued from intense wildfires.
Three mothers, their three daughters and two adult males were freed in a reserve in the west of the island on Friday.
Indonesian wildlife authorities rescued 46 of the apes, which are critically endangered, before fires tore through their habitat in August and September.

articles.title: Pennsylvania shooter who killed eight was a grandfather, says slain child’s dad
articles.summary:
Father of toddler killed in Erie mass shooting says reported gunman never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary

The man who killed eight people, before turning the gun on himself, in a

blocks.text: The man who killed eight people, before turning the gun on himself, in a mass shooting in a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday was a grandfather who had not shown signs that he was capable of such violence, according to people who knew the shooter.
A man whose toddler was among those killed said on Sunday that the man never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary, the Associated Press reports.

“I think that was a front for him,” said Julius Windham during a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting. Windham’s one-year-old daughter, Amarianna; her pregnant mother; and the woman’s five-year-old son and unborn baby were among the victims.
“Him every day, him smiling and being just – you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said.

The 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but the Erie police chief, Rick Lorah, said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either.

Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 pm on Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the slain woman and children and the words “Forever in my heart”.
“Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now,” Windham said. “But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody.”

“We don’t want that dark memory to be what defines their lives in this world,” a family friend told Cleveland 19 News. “How do you even fathom something like this? How will you go home and tell your kids: ‘Hey, your mom, your siblings, your uncles and everybody else just got murdered by your grandpa?’”

Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them before returning inside.

blocks.caption: Firefighters work outside the home where nine members of a family were killed in a mass shooting on Saturday in Erie, Pennsylvania. Photograph: Jeff Swensen/Getty Images

blocks.text: Responding officers found the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of the five-year-old boy and one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.
“Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at a news conference.
“But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole,” he said.
Erie is about 120 miles (190km) north of Pittsburgh.
after newsletter promotion
Lorah declined to discuss motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.
“They knew something was going on at that house,” Lorah said. “We have to figure out what that is.”

Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, told the Associated Press they have known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter “was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything”.

“They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?” Debra Eller said. “Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?”
The Erie shooting was reminiscent of a 1982 massacre in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, in which a man killed 13 people, including five of his own children.
At a news conference on Saturday, Erie’s mayor, Daria Devlin, addressed a portion of her remarks directly to the victims’ families.

“I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier ... Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.”
“My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community,” said Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, in a post on X on Saturday.

articles.title: Iconic Australian band Powderfinger announce first tour in 17 years
articles.summary: The band, who announced their reunion last week, say they are "absolutely ecstatic" to be playing together again.

blocks.text: Powderfinger, one of Australia's best loved rock bands, has unveiled details of a comeback tour – to take place 17 years after they broke up.
The Brisbane-based group, who confirmed their reunion last week, will kick off with four nights in their home city next September.
They will then play another 14 shows across Cairns, Sydney, Adelaide, Perth and Melbourne, with all gigs to be staged in a "stadium sized big-top" tent.
In a statement on Monday the band said they were "absolutely ecstatic" to be getting together and playing again.
"Over the years there have been tons of suggestions for us to go back on the road but, until now, it never felt quite right or lined up for all of us," they said.
"We have always been so grateful for the continued support from our long-term fans and over the years we've picked up a lot of new ones who have never seen us play."

"People often tell us that our music is connected to their most treasured and joyous memories," they added. "We hope to spread a little more of that joy when we make our way around the country with some of Australia's best established and upcoming talent, and to make some new memories for us all."
The tour schedule of only playing on Friday and Saturday nights is similar to that adopted by Oasis in their world tour last year. No gigs outside of Australia have yet been announced.

Powderfinger released seven studio albums during their career including 2000's Odyssey Number Five which was voted best Australian album of all time by listeners of Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) music station Triple J in 2011.
That included the single My Happiness, which was voted sixth best Australian song of all time by the same station in 2025. The group's other hits include On My Mind and These Days and Sunsets.
Since the band split, frontman Bernard Fanning has maintained a solo career while bassist John Collins has gone on to open two of Brisbane's largest live music venues.

articles.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
articles.summary: Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have criticised the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.

Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.
That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.
The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.
As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.

This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.
They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".
The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.
Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.

Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.
Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.
The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.
Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, which amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.

Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

articles.title: American ranchers wrestle with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump
articles.summary: Many farmers in states that backed the president say they are being hit from all sides, with the crucial midterm elections just weeks away.

blocks.text: Image source, Yvette Mannon
Rancher Yvette Mannon was already dealing with a destructive wildfire and rising fuel costs before the US announced new foreign beef imports
BySheila Flynn
Senior US Reporter, Nebraska
Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year.

In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines.
Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed.
With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000.

On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year.

Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold.
The cattle market tanked immediately.
'It felt like a betrayal'
"So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry."
"It just felt like a betrayal," she said.

Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain.
That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances.
Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race.

Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cattle farming is big business in Nebraska - where ranchers say they are facing soaring costs

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Cattle farming is big business in Nebraska - where ranchers say they are facing soaring costs

The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices.
And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive.
Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle.
"All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas.

Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing.

Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jake Wolfinger, 45, says he is frustrated with the way Trump has intervened in the beef market - but believes the President

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Lori Potter
Jake Wolfinger, 45, says he is frustrated with the way Trump has intervened in the beef market - but believes the President

The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry.
But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning.

"Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head.
Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day.
"It really makes a guy think," he said.
A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left.
But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market.
"People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said.
'People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business'
Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall.
"The daily upcharge… is kind of painful," he said.
"I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit."
Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago.
But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said.
He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit," said Duane Kimball

blocks.text: "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit," said Duane Kimball
Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms.
But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate.

That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago.
Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper.
He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts.
That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry.
"Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News.

An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy".
Now, he said, "I think he's been anything but practical".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jim Jenkins says he is incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry

blocks.text: Jim Jenkins says he is incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry
But for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt.
"We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it."
But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction".

Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things".
But Cantrell believes Trump has been the "best president overall". His establishment of DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency - for example, was exactly what he felt the country needed.
"Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Don Cantrell says he believes Trump has been the "best president overall" - citing his efforts to "cut government waste"

blocks.text: Don Cantrell says he believes Trump has been the "best president overall" - citing his efforts to "cut government waste"
Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions.
"I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said.
Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture."
Still, the economic realities are hard to ignore, he said.

Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later.

But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Don Batie, 67, says he has had to abandon his dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter

blocks.text: Don Batie, 67, says he has had to abandon his dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter
"It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in.
He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers.
"I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbers… I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'"
Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state.
"They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cattle still need to be bought and sold, and vast ranches - many multi-generational - operate throughout the state

blocks.text: Image source, Lori Potter
Cattle still need to be bought and sold, and vast ranches - many multi-generational - operate throughout the state
All over Nebraska, however, the industry soldiers on.
On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction.
Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - don not pause for politics.
Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude.
"People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it."

articles.title: Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
articles.summary: After analysing 1,500 videos and images of the Raila Odinga memorial, Africa Eye finds that those killed were far from the scuffles.

blocks.text: Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.

During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."

Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.

The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.

After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.
In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.

Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.

Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.

Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia: Second strike kills at least 1 at Riyadh airport
articles.summary: Sunday's strike came as the King Khalid International Airport remained closed after a deadly attack on Saturday, and after a warning from Houthi rebels in Yemen that "worse is yet to come." Dammam…
articles.byline: Zac Crellin, Matt Ford, Karl Sexton

image.caption: Riyadh airport will be closed until at least Sunday night [FILE: 2019]Image: Valery Sharifulin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: At least one person was killed and 11 others were injured in a stike on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Sunday, a day after a similar attack killed 12 and injured hundreds.
"King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was subjected to a new attack on Sunday afternoon," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement.
It later confirmed that the individual killed in the Sunday attack was a Pakistani national.

A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said that a cruise missile had been intercepted by air defense systems in the vicinity of the airport, but no further details were immediately available.
The Houthis later claimed responsibility for the strikes, saying they had "carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones."
A spokesman said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport in the east of the country and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco.
Later on Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed an attack on Dammam airport.
Houthis warn airlines after deadly Riyadh airport strike
Houthis warn airlines to avoid Saudi Arabia
The latest Houthi strikes also came just hours after the rebel group warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports.

"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces," read a statement released by the group on social media. It added that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina would not be targeted.
"We ‌urge everyone to take our warnings seriously," the statement continued, stating: "Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."
What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack?
Why are Saudi airports being targeted?

Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the rebels seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, including around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Houthi-run health authority claimed this weekend that 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in the last five weeks, 60% of them women and children. Earlier on Sunday, it said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.
The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV also reported that Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims.

"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the Houthi-run Foreign Ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah TV on Sunday, adding that its ​actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.
What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attacks?

The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime."
The Houthi strikes on Riyadh come amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure.
The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.
The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies, have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago.

While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis.
Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis?
How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes?
US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable."
Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels.
On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation."

"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shock waves sent through the world," von der Leyen said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".
"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X.

UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.
Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means."
Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks.
Why can't the Saudis defeat the Houthis?

articles.title: UK's Burnham accuses Russia of meddling in Brexit vote
articles.summary: The UK prime minister called for voters in Europe to be made fully aware of Russia's attempts to influence politics.

image.caption: 'Bregret' is growing in the UK; 60% of voters now think leaving was a mistake [FILE: June 2026] Image: Birgit Maaß/DW

blocks.text: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Sunday became the first British leader to openly complain of Russian tampering in the Brexit referendum a decade ago.
Burnham, who took on the role in July from Keir Starmer, thinks leaving the European Union did "more harm than good" and has opened the door to closer ties, including possibly rejoining the bloc.
What did Burnham say?
Burnham told The Rest Is Politics podcast that he had posed the question upon first arriving in Downing Street, and was given a "clear answer that yes, there was [a link to Russian interference]."
He did not provide evidence of the Kremlin's efforts to influence the June 2016 vote, where the UK decided to leave the EU by a 52% to 48% majority.
With the rise of far-right parties in the UK and across the EU, Burnham ​said voters needed better information about efforts by rogue states to disrupt their democracies.

"These things are important now to put clearly on the ​record, and I believe, ‌help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," he said.
Burnham described how German Chancellor Friedrich Merz had told him during talks in Berlin this week that the AfD is "clearly linked to Russia — funded, I believe.”
"There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics,” Burnham added.

blocks.caption: Burnham (right) met German Chancellor Merz in Berlin this weekImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Leaver' Johnson denied Russian meddling
Burnham's Brexit remarks contrast with former Prime Minister Boris Johnson, who campaigned to leave the EU. In 2020, Johnson said ​there was no evidence of Russian sway.
The UK Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee found in 2020 that the government had failed to fully assess how Russian state-run media and “troll” accounts could have impacted the vote.
In its report, the Committee also found the Kremlin sought to influence Scotland's 2014 independence referendum, which was rejected by voters.

The UK's intelligence agencies believe Russia continues to spread disinformation to undermine public trust, alongside cyberattacks, sabotage and espionage. They say the issue is getting worse and is often aided by artificial intelligence (AI).
Russia has long denied meddling in other countries' elections or referendums.
After the Brexit vote, it cast some British politicians as gripped by anti-Russian hysteria.
Brexit balance sheet: why the UK economy is faltering
How have UK attitudes toward Brexit changed?
Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.
Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave. Last month, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

Last month, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.
EU officials have welcomed the change in tone from London, while France and Spain have spoken positively about closer ties, including rejoining.

Some experts remain skeptical, however. Professor Iain Begg of the London School of Economics thinks rejoining would reopen deep political divisions, be complicated from both the EU and UK sides and likely take years.

articles.title: Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
articles.summary: The US president made the announcement in a social media post, which was an apparent surprise to Ukraine and Russia is yet to comment.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has said Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire".
Moscow is yet to comment on the announcement and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told US media it was "news to me".
Trump also recently announced a US deal to import Russian diesel, in an attempt to bring the fuel price down ahead of the midterm elections.
The price of diesel in the US has been high since the start of the war with Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The BBC's Joe Inwood examines Trump's announcement and what might mean for the president ahead of the midterm election.

articles.title: Turkey gravy brand sold in Canada recalled due to undeclared mustard
articles.summary: A brand of turkey gravy sold in Canada has been recalled because it contains undeclared mustard.

image.caption: A gravy boat is shown in a file image. Kevin's Natural Foods turkey gravy has been recalled in Canada because the product contains mustard, which is not included on its label, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency says. (Matthew Mead/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba
A brand of turkey gravy sold in Canada has been recalled because it contains undeclared mustard.
Kevin's Natural Foods turkey gravy sold in Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan
Kevin's Natural Foods turkey gravy is sold in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency says the product contains mustard, which is not included on its label.
The agency says the recall was triggered by the company and there have been no reported reactions associated with the product.
It says the turkey gravy should not be consumed by anyone who is allergic or sensitive to mustard and is advising customers not to distribute or sell it.
The agency is investigating and says it is verifying that the product is being removed from the marketplace.
Health Canada recognizes mustard as a common food allergen.

articles.title: Air strikes kill dozens of gold miners on Sudan-Egypt border
articles.summary: A Sudan-based rights group said 72 people were killed in a remote, disputed area known for illegal gold mining.

image.caption: A UN report found that half of the gold mined in Sudan is smuggled out of the countryImage: Ashraf Shazly/AFP

blocks.text: At least 72 workers were killed in air strikes on a disputed border area between Sudan and Egypt that targeted artisanal gold miners, a human rights group said Sunday.
The attack, south of the remote Halayeb triangle, east of the River Nile, is the second of its kind this year.
It comes amid growing concern in Egypt over large-scale displacement from the three-and-a-half-year conflict in Sudan, which has spurred a cross-border exodus.
What do we know?
The Sudan-based Emergency Lawyers, a human rights and legal advocacy organization, said the attack occurred on Saturday in rugged and mountainous territory that it said lies within Sudan.
The Halayeb triangle, which is claimed by both Egypt and Sudan, is known for mining and the gold trade, along with other illicit goods and human trafficking.
The rights group accused the Egyptian air force of carrying out the strikes.
"The repeated attacks on the gold- and mineral-rich border regions reflect a desire by Egyptian authorities to expand and assert control over Sudan's natural resources," it claimed.
Egypt has yet to comment on the strikes, but has previously admitted conducting a "large-scale operation" against illegal gold mining within its borders.
Independent verification remains difficult because of the remote location.

blocks.caption: Child labor is widespread in Sudan's dangerous gold mining sectorImage: Interpol/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Death toll expected to rise

Sudan Doctors Network warned on Facebook of an expected increase in the number of casualties "due to the severity of some injuries and the difficulties in accessing medical care and essential services in the region."
One survivor told the AFP news agency there were thousands of people working at the remote site when it was hit.
"After the air strike, people scattered. Some people came to Al-Ansary [gold] market, others went in the other direction. That's why no one knows exactly how many were killed," he said.
Strikes tied to war's gold economy
Sudan's civil war between Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's military junta and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has killed more than 200,000 people and triggered a severe humanitarian crisis.
Despite backing Sudan's army chief al-Burhan, Egypt considers the war at its border a threat to its security.

The RSF has funded its operations by smuggling thousands of tons of gold from Sudan's Darfur and Kordofan regions. According to the UK-based think tank Chatham House, as much as 60% of unofficial gold exports end up in Egypt.
Sudan's civil war — the limits of humanitarian aid
In June, air strikes on mining sites in the same border area were followed by a large-scale Egyptian security operation.
Hundreds of people, including foreigners, were arrested, accused of illegal gold mining and smuggling.

articles.title: Who are the Ukrainian 'volunteers' under Russian command?
articles.summary: Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian "volunteers." But veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts.

image.caption: Russian media reports say it has numerous military formations made up of former Ukrainian soldiersImage: Kaskad

blocks.text: Pavlo Oliynyk, 25, says he joined enemy forces to escape Russian captivity. Before his capture in the Donbas region in 2024, he was a senior lieutenant for Ukraine's armed forces.

As a prisoner of war (POW), he says he was electrocuted, beaten and psychologically tortured. So when he received the offer to join the Maksym Kryvonis battalion — named after a famous 17th-century Cossack commander — he accepted.
Oliynyk says he wanted to use this opportunity to reach the front lines, so he could escape to Ukrainian-controlled territory. DW was able to contact Oliynyk through his lawyer.
'Ukrainian volunteers' consist mostly of POWs

Reports of Russian combat units consisting of Ukrainian prisoners of war and former service members of Ukraine's armed forces began emerging in late 2022. Several detachments were initially formed and in August 2026, they were merged into the so-called "Ukrainian Volunteer Special Forces Brigade."

blocks.caption: Pavlo Oliynyk says he defected to Russian forces in order to escape captivityImage: Privatarchiv

blocks.text: Of the individual units, the Maksym Kryvonis battalion has perhaps drawn the most public attention for having evidently taken part in combat. Its true size is unknown — Russian media reports claim about 200 fighters while available footage only suggests several dozen.

An investigative team of the Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne has identified over 30 members and confirmed they are all former Ukrainian servicemen, captured by Russian forces between 2023 and 2024.
An 'imitation' of Russian legions fighting for Ukraine

Pavel Luzin, an expert for Russian foreign policy and defense at the Center for European Policy Analysis, believes these units are an "imitation" of the Russian Volunteer Corps and the Freedom of Russia Legion — units in the Ukrainian armed forces, consisting of Russian citizens — and an attempt by Moscow to distract from the fact that these units exist in the first place. Ukrainian intelligence services tend to agree.

"It bothers them that Russians would fight on Ukraine's side, but Ukrainians won't fight on Russia's side," Yevhen Shybalov, author and veteran of the war in Ukraine, told DW. He added that Russian troops have never tried to hide the fact that Russian volunteer units in Ukrainian ranks were the main reason Russian forces wanted to create Ukrainian units for their own ranks.
Just how voluntary are these combat units?
In 2025, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) reported that 95% of the released Ukrainian POWs interviewed reported torture or ill-treatment during Russian captivity.

Bill Wiley, executive director of the NGO Commission for International Justice and Accountability, said the physical and psychological state of the returned combatants raises serious doubts that their recruitment was voluntary. Mykhailo Savva of the Center for Civil Liberties, a Kyiv-based human rights organization, points to the criminal procedures running against several of the battalion members, which he said indicates that these suggest the combatants had switched sides voluntarily.

But where to draw the line between voluntary and involuntary recruitment? The war veteran and human rights activist Maksym Butkevych, who spent 28 months as a prisoner of war, said the conditions in Russian captivity make that line hard to distinguish. On the one hand, he said, there is a constant atmosphere of pressure, and on the other hand, it's not implausible that some prisoners defected out of ideological proximity.
How were Ukrainian prisoners made to join Russian forces?

Butkevych told DW that between 2022 and 2023, all Ukrainian prisoners of war had received offers, "more or less persistently," to join the Russian army. In his case, he recounted, it was after he had been severely mistreated.
"They showed us they could do anything they wanted to us," he explained, "which was why we should agree to everything."

The veteran Shybalov reported similar experiences, speaking of attempts to force confessions of war crimes, or to recruit members for Russia's intelligence services. He told DW all prisoners were first interrogated and then made certain propositions under duress.

"You can torture people to get them to confess, but there comes the difficult moment when you need to give them a weapon," he said. "That's why it's more about psychological pressure, and forcing voluntary compliance."
Butkevych confirmed these accounts with his own tales. But neither veteran has ever met someone willing to join Russian units, they said.
What happens after conscription?
Oliynyk, from the Maksym Kryvonis battalion, said he initially turned down multiple bids to join Russian forces. He said he only accepted the fourth offer so he could flee.

He claimed he didn't sign official Defense Ministry paperwork, but a private contract with an individual offering military services. Afterwards, he said, he was brought to a room where he heard lectures and saw videos and photos he was later asked to retell.
Putin's foreign fighters
Control and mistreatment
Oliynyk said fellow service members in the Maksym Kryvonis battalion consisted both of those who had switched sides of their own volition, and those who had been forced.

In a video circulating online that appears to be of a trial in Ukraine, he also says former Ukrainian POWs in the unit were followed and guarded by mercenaries of the private Russian military company Redut. In the same video, he also speaks of beatings and torture, and receiving monthly wages in envelopes handed out by a member of Russia's military intelligence.

Oliynyk told DW he had been given a phone, but that he was too scared to call anyone in Ukraine because it was under constant surveillance. He denied having fought against Ukrainians, as he fled in March 2025 before his first deployment in the Donetsk province. After running across a field, he said he spent two days hiding from drones in basements and houses before making contact with Ukrainian fighters.
Now, Oliynyk has been in detention in Ukraine for nearly two years while authorities investigate possible treason. He has yet to be formally charged.
Sergey Nikitin contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of improper conduct
articles.summary:
Senior official says president and US secretary of state are ‘extremely pissed off’ by conduct of US envoy to Greece

Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, are considering…

blocks.text: Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, are considering firing US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.

A senior US official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s federal holiday.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled.

In a series of stories, the Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the US embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her.
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”

But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm.

“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied.

A second US official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the state department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.

The second official could not say if a formal IG investigation had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.
The state department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.

The top two Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House committee for oversight and government reform, Robert Garcia, Democrat of California, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.

Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.

While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.

The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.

Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr.

articles.title: Hurricane Simon hits Mexico's Pacific coast, slamming towns and resorts
articles.summary: Hurricane Simon was pounding Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 4 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre…

image.caption: A child wades through a flooded street as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing heavy rain and strong winds to Manzanillo, Mexico, on Sunday. (Daniel Becerril/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·Updated

Hurricane Simon was pounding Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 4 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.
Hurricane specialist says 'life-threatening' storm surge expected

Simon's eye was moving northward just off the coast, and forecasters at the U.S. National Hurricane Center said it's not clear if it will make landfall. This could mean Simon maintains its extremely dangerous strength, sustaining winds of 240 km/h.

That's not good news for people in the Puerto Vallarta area, a popular destination for Canadian tourists. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.

At daybreak, Simon was centered about 175 kilometres south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, and moving north-northwest at a relatively slow eight km/h. A senior Hurricane Center specialist, Phillippe Pappin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico was the most likely place for landfall.
"Simon is very close to the coast of Mexico this morning," Pappin told The Associated Press on Sunday.
"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Pappin said.

"They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."

items: Category 4 Hurricane Simon barrels toward Mexico
Hurricane Simon forecast to get much stronger as it heads to Mexico's Pacific Coast

blocks.text: As for predicting whether or not Simon will make landfall, "it's a little tricky right now" to forecast, since the eye "is basically moving very close or parallel to the coast currently," Pappin said. But he predicted that Cabo Corrientes is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system on Sunday.
Waves hit the shore in Manzanillo on Sunday. (Daniel Becerril/Reuters)
Heavy rainfall elsewhere

Meanwhile, the hurricane was dumping rain over parts of southwestern Mexico. It could bring 25 to 50 centimetres of rain in many places, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 76 centimetres. "This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the centre warned.

Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers as well as visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.
On Saturday, just ahead of the worst weather, convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows.
A man removes water from a building in Manzanillo on Sunday. (Daniel Becerril/Reuters)

The hurricane centre expected a dangerous storm surge along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the centre makes landfall. The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.
Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who, along with his wife, still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.
"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do. "I just don't know what to expect."

articles.title: Children among at least 139 dead after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti coast
articles.summary: At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in East Africa, the International Organization for Migration said…

image.caption: This image provided by the International Organization for Migration shows a boat after it capsized near Guhere, Djibouti, on Saturday. (Alexandre Coissac/International Organization for Migration/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in East Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday.
Toll only includes those buried by authorities, says UN migration agency

That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves, but they won't be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, told The Associated Press.
"What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation," Coissac said. "They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened."
Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, "mainly because it was overcrowded."
"The local authorities did their best," Coissac said, "but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore."
He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue centre in Obock where they would receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support.
A pair of trousers believed to belong to a migrant lies on the shore near Guhere. (Kennedy Omondi Okoth/International Organization for Migration/Reuters)
"They're all in a state of shock," said Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday. "I tried to talk to some of them, but it's very difficult."

Some of the migrants in the IOM centre are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive.

At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.

The death toll from the #Djibouti shipwreck has risen to 139, with 84 people still missing. As search and recovery efforts continue, IOM is providing emergency assistance to survivors. Every life lost is one too many. Read the latest updates here: https://t.co/LJjeAtSer2 https://t.co/VXfiv3TeFA—UNmigration
The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said.
The Geneva-based UN migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise.
Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing.
'Safe and legal pathways save lives'

Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait toward Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement.
That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait.
"This is a devastating loss of life," said Coissac. "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities."
Members of the International Organization for Migration receive migrants near Guhere. (Kennedy Omondi Okoth/International Organization for Migration/Reuters)

In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

That's the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: the tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia.

blocks.text: Over 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project.

"No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way," IOM director general Amy Pope said. "We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down."

Lasik MD's spokesperson Jessica Lukian Papineau said Bashour was suspended immediately that night, and all his surgeries were reassigned to other physicians the next morning. That case is due in court next year, and no charges have officially been laid against Bashour.
Court documents describe Dr. Mounir Bashour as recruiter and go-between for escort agency's boss

Lasik MD announced Saturday that it has fired one of its surgeons, Dr. Mounir Bashour, who worked for the company in Montreal and several locations in Ontario including Toronto and Ottawa for over 20 years, according to Radio-Canada.
Bashour's name came up amid a host of troubling revelations during this week's Enquête show on Radio-Canada.

The first mention of his name was in court documents, in connection with a Montreal police investigation into an escort agency called XO, which involved stings and surveillance operations resulting in the dismantling of the network last winter.
The case is due in court next year, and no charges have been laid against Bashour.

Lasik MD's spokesperson Jessica Lukian Papineau said in a statement the company was deeply shaken by the show's reporting. She said Bashour was suspended immediately that night, and that all his upcoming surgeries were reassigned to other physicians the next morning.
"Our priority remains with our patients and employees," she wrote.

articles.title: Poland detains man suspected of planning assassination of PM Tusk
articles.summary: Police received credible information about possible attacks against Donald Tusk and his defence minister.

blocks.text: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a man accused of plotting an assassination attack against him and his defence minister has been detained.
The interior ministry earlier reported that police had received credible information about possible attacks against Tusk and Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.
Security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about the planned attacks, with a spokesman saying officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".
Tusk thanked the police for "swift and decisive action" in arresting the suspect.
The suspect was arrested in the Lower Silesia region and is a Polish national, Jacek Dobrzynski, a spokesman for the Special Services Coordinator told local media.
"In this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out," he said.

The plan was uncovered when an email with information about the potential attack was forwarded to police by the State Protection Service, which is responsible for ministers' security, Interior Ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka said.
Tusk has been Polish prime minister since 2023 after previously holding the office from 2007 to 2014.
He served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed: Democrats must ‘win by massive numbers’ to fend off Trump election denial
articles.summary:
Democratic Senate candidate’s remarks come as Trump has long baselessly claimed his 2020 election loss was stolen

Democrats must…

blocks.text: Democrats must “win by massive numbers” during November’s federal midterm elections because Donald Trump and his Republican allies are bound to try to sow doubt about the integrity of the results, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said on Sunday.

El-Sayed’s comments on NBC’s Meet the Press came with the Democrats favored to win control of the House of Representatives during the 3 November midterms – and polls show that the party could also win Senate seats in states that traditionally elect Republicans and gain a majority there, too.
Meanwhile, Trump has long baselessly maintained that the 2020 presidential election which he lost as an incumbent to Joe Biden was stolen by fraudsters.
He also gave a primetime speech in July in which he made unverified claims about Chinese interference in the election, and he fired members of an independent federal election commission.

When asked later by a rightwing broadcaster whether the president might declare a national security emergency pertaining to elections for the midterms, Trump ignited alarm among some observers by replying: “Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?”
The New York Times, meanwhile, reported that Trump had cast doubt on elections on 440 days of his second presidency, which began in early 2025.

As such, on NBC’s Meet the Press Sunday, El-Sayed was asked whether Democrats needed to turn out in such numbers in November that the election would be “too big to rig” – as it had recently been put by former vice-president Kamala Harris, who lost the 2024 White House election to Trump.
“Donald Trump has already threatened to do what he did in 2020, which is deny the outcomes of an election,” El-Sayed said. “So, yes, we have to win by massive numbers.”
The Cook Political Report revised its predictions on Tuesday and declared that “A Senate Majority is Squarely in Democrats’ Sights”.
A recent New York Times and Siena University poll found Democratic Senate candidates leading in Alaska, Ohio and Texas, states that Trump won by double digits in 2024.
The poll showed El-Sayed leading Republican candidate Mike Rogers by five points.

El-Sayed on Sunday’s Meet the Press alluded to how Rogers had also claimed that a 2024 US Senate election which he lost to Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, was stolen from him – after first having conceded the race.
Rogers in November 2025 was reported to have said at events that a single van carrying fraudulent ballots in Detroit cost him the race against Slotkin.
“The guy … I’m running against insinuates that he didn’t actually lose,” El-Sayed said to Kristen Welker. “That’s the guy I’m running against right now.”

articles.title: Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to boost domestic European industry
articles.summary:
Oliver Blume says ‘Made in Europe’ rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’

The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its…

blocks.text: The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals.
Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week.

The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries.

Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs. Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”.

The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.

Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China.
On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.
Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints.
“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said.
Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The new all-electric ID Tiguan. Photograph: Volkswagen AG

blocks.text: Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.”
Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin.
Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”.

The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes.
On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.
