Anastasia says she completed her first two surrogacies in Russia, and her third — for a Japanese couple, brokered through the branch office of a Moscow clinic — in Georgia. Like many surrogate mothers, she went home to Russia after the embryo was implanted, and returned to Georgia when she was 22 weeks pregnant.

"I live in an apartment with another surrogate mother who carried twins to term. This program was the easiest and most practical one for me, but maybe I just got lucky with the right clinic," Anastasia told DW. "Other women who gave birth in Georgia told me they had difficulties. For example, after giving birth, they had to wait a long time before they were paid." She says she's ready to become a surrogate mother again.

Estimates vary, but there are about 19 clinics that offer such services across Georgia. And at around €45,000 ($50,400) to €55,000, the average service costs for agencies in Tbilisi or Batumi are only about a third of what agencies in other countries charge.
Several surrogate mothers who gave birth in Georgian clinics told DW that their average salary was between €18,000 and €28,000, with premiums added for birthing twins, for example.
Surrogate mothers from Ukraine in demand

Daniel and Olga told DW that they spent months looking for surrogacy agency in Georgia. "Pretty soon, we had access to a list of women from Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Georgia, and were given a detailed description of the process, along with the contact information of lawyers who could help take care of the formalities," they recount. "We were a little concerned that not every agency could give clear answers about the health of some of the surrogate mothers."

Both work in the medical field, and Olga says perhaps some of their questions about the physical health and possible genetic disorders might have been too probing. "We picked a 30-year-old woman from Ukraine who had already been a surrogate mother once for a European couple," she says. The Russian-Georgian agency set up half-hour long Zoom call, "but that hardly seemed enough to make a final decision," Olga adds.

In the spring of 2024, the married couple traveled to Georgia's capital to meet Elena (her name has been changed to protect her identity). Following a long discussion, the agency had seemed reluctant when they agreed to bring her to Tbilisi for the meeting. Elena made a good first impression on the couple from Hamburg, showing them pictures of her children and telling them she wanted to use the money she earned to renovate her apartment.

"They had initially told us that the surrogate would spent the entire pregnancy living in a rented apartment in Tbilisi," Olga and Daniel tell DW. "But then we found out that Elena was going back home for a few months after the embryo was implanted, back to Ukraine, where there's war."
Human rights experts criticize legislation

Georgian laws have a weak spot, the human rights lawyer Nino Bogveradze tells DW: They only regulate the relationship between the surrogate mothers, the intended parents, and the clinics, but they do not consider the roles that agencies play.

In Georgia, surrogate mothers have limited rights. Most concerns related to their pregnancy, medical care or payment are not regulated by national law but in contracts between the involved parties. And the state does not set minimum standards for social guarantees or contractual terms.
Surrogacy laws and rules vary widely across Africa

After an embryo has been implanted, surrogate mothers are not allowed to keep the child, leave the program, or end the pregnancy. Several human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the International Women's Health Coalition say the established practice in Georgia violates women's rights to reproductive self-determination.
Agencies guided by material interests

"Agencies often speak of their special mission to help people have the child they've been dreaming of," Olga Doletskaya from the University of Leeds tell DW. "But in reality, they're primarily driven by financial interests. And that's why they exploit the precarious situation of surrogate mothers, and pressure intended parents."

Olga and Daniel from Hamburg agree. "We were constantly being made to understand that we should decide as quickly as possible. We had to hurry because apparently several other couples were also interested in our surrogate," Olga says.

And the agency kept stressing that it had paid out of pocket for bringing the potential surrogate mother to Georgia, despite that not being contractually agreed. "At some point, a representative noticed my emotional state and asked me how long I wanted to remain childless," Olga recounts. "I felt like I was being manipulated."
The couple returned to Germany with mixed feelings and decided to shelve the idea of employing a surrogate mother — at least, for now.
Mark Sheider and Asja Lokina contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Russian.

articles.title: Germany's population is shrinking, but not everywhere
articles.summary: By 2045, Germany will have more older people, fewer workers and a smaller population overall. Yet some regions will defy this trend. Their success depends on how much they have to offer.

image.caption: Some areas in Germany will see population numbers dwindleImage: Jens Kalaene/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's population is expected to decline from 83.5 million in 2025 to around 81.8 million by 2045, according to a new study from the Berlin Institute for Population and Development (Berlin-Institut für Bevölkerung und Entwicklung), in collaboration with the Wüstenrot Foundation, a non-profit that supports research on housing, urban development, and social change.

The decline in population alone is not the central challenge. More significant is the continuing rise in the number of retirees alongside a steadily shrinking workforce. Across Germany, the working-age population is projected to decrease by 4.7% by 2045.

"The baby boomer generation is retiring, while significantly smaller cohorts are following. Birth rates are falling, and immigration is not sufficient to offset the growing surplus of deaths over births," said Institute President Catherina Hinz when presenting the study in Berlin.
The term "baby boomers" refers to those born in the 1960s, when annual births exceeded one million. Thereafter, the birth rate fell sharply, effectively halving.
The economy matters

Germany's population may be shrinking, but according to the study, this trend is far from uniform across the country. In the years ahead, a region's economic attractiveness, and the financial strength that comes with it, will become even more important than it is today.

"Some regions will lose substantial numbers of residents and workers in the years ahead, while others continue to grow. Even within eastern Germany, southern Germany, and rural areas, the demographic and economic divide is widening," said Hinz.

"Demographic change is unfolding before our very eyes, and its effects are being felt across the country," Hinz added. "Its consequences can still be mitigated, but they can no longer be avoided. And the longer we wait, the narrower our scope for action will become."

Hinz's warning is echoed by Frederick Sixtus of the Berlin Institute. Almost every region now records more deaths than births, he notes, a consequence of decades of low birth rates. The implication is clear: Migration, both inward and outward, now shapes a region's demographic trajectory. Over recent decades, immigration from abroad has repeatedly helped stabilize population trends. Yet migration alone is no longer enough to halt the aging of society.

According to the study, several factors are critical if a region is to remain attractive to people relocating from abroad or from other parts of Germany: High-quality jobs offering good pay and working conditions, a sufficient supply of skilled workers for local businesses, financially robust municipalities, reliable childcare, and efficient transport and mobility infrastructure.
Berlin leads the way

Many major cities are expected to continue to grow in the years ahead, according to Manuel Slupina of the Wüstenrot Foundation. The study projects that Berlin will lead the way, with the capital's population increasing by almost 10% by 2045. Other cities expected to attract people include Hamburg, Frankfurt am Main, Munich, and Düsseldorf in western Germany, as well as Leipzig, Dresden, and Potsdam in the east.

The study's authors argue that the familiar distinction between urban and rural areas does not hold true everywhere. The hinterlands of many major cities are also expected to grow. While young people are increasingly drawn to metropolitan centers, families with children tend to settle in the surrounding areas. Among the places likely to lose population are several large cities in western Germany, including Bremen, Duisburg, Dortmund, and Kaiserslautern, whose economic appeal has gradually diminished. At the bottom of the ranking are many sparsely populated regions, a large number of them in eastern Germany.
Competition for talent

Twelve of the 20 districts and independent cities with the weakest overall ratings are now located in eastern Germany, up from five in the previous assessment in 2019. According to the study, these regions are also expected to see the steepest declines in their working-age populations, with losses of up to 18% by 2045. The authors conclude that competition for workers is therefore set to become one of the key demographic challenges of the decades ahead.

In this competition, the southern German states of Bavariaand Baden-Württemberg are regarded as having the strongest prospects. Bavaria ranks particularly highly thanks to its robust economy, which is thriving across much of the state, and its strong labor market. Women, older people, and people without German citizenship are also more likely to be employed in Bavaria than elsewhere. The ranking shows that economically successful regions are more effective at integrating different population groups into the labor market than weaker ones.
Why Germans want children but are having fewer babies
Policymakers must find local solutions
Under Germany's constitution, the country is committed to ensuring that people enjoy comparable opportunities, and with them the prospect of a good life, regardless of where they live.

The researchers offer clear recommendations to policymakers. They argue that the focus must be on addressing structural challenges and regional disparities. "What may be the right response for a growing major city is not necessarily the right one for a shrinking rural district," says Slupina. Tailor-made solutions are needed, but they require the right framework conditions. "There needs to be less rigid regulation, more scope for local initiative, and greater financial resources, especially for municipalities and those actively engaged at the local level." Slupina's message is clear: Regions should be trusted to shape their own futures.

Local authorities would no doubt welcome that. For years, mayors and district administrators have been calling for greater financial autonomy. They are currently seeking a larger share of overall tax revenues for municipalities. The federal government and the states, however, argue that they face budgetary constraints of their own. Yet both sides recognize that, sooner or later, Germany will have little choice but to reform its system of fiscal federalism.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: ‘It was a terrible thing’: Panama declares state of emergency as quake aftershocks rattle communities
articles.summary:
More than 100 aftershocks as high as magnitude-5.8 recorded after two quakes toppled buildings and prompted evacuations

Panama’s government has declared a state of emergency on Saturday as…

blocks.text: Panama’s government has declared a state of emergency on Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours.
Officials did not attribute any deaths to Friday’s 7.7- and 6.6-magnitude earthquakes, but reported damages in all 10 of Panama’s provinces and two Indigenous territories.

The earthquakes toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.

The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centred about 10km (6 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the US Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10km (6 miles).

blocks.caption: A car sits crushed beneath debris from a collapsed building in Penonome, Panama. Photograph: Enea Lebrun/Reuters

blocks.text: The presidential minister, Juan Carlos Orillac, announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, healthcare facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities.
Malitzie Rivera, the deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, said 27 people had been reported with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate.
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos.

About 420 homes and the same number of public schools had been damaged, according to the Civil Protection agency. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes.

In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64km (40 miles) north-east of the epicentre, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government’s guidance on what to do next.

“We’ve been here since 1 pm yesterday; we haven’t moved,” Tony Jiménez, whose home partially collapsed, said, while sitting with relatives under a tent. “It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense – truly intense.”

blocks.caption: Elodia Oliva (94) rests in a park in downtown Tonosi, Panama, on Saturday.  Photograph: Bienvenido Velasco/EPA

blocks.text: Officials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage.

That the country appeared to have avoided widespread deaths could be due to its strict building codes, especially governing the construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdés, the head of the seismology department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.

Messages of support and offers of assistance were sent from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others.

The US Department of State on Saturday said it mobilised a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments. The US government also pledged $5m for humanitarian assistance.
The US military’s southern command said two helicopters, supported by the state department’s drug-control bureau, had delivered 2,000 pounds (907kg) of food to people affected by the earthquakes.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia extends airport closure and moves Riyadh schools online after deadly strike

image.caption: People gather outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. (The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia on Sunday kept its main international airport closed and moved Riyadh schools online as Yemen's Houthi rebels threatened new strikes across the kingdom, a day after a missile attack killed 12 people and wounded more than 300.

Saturday's strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh marked a major escalation in the war between Yemen's Iran's-backed Houthis and the kingdom and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war.

U.S. President Donald Trump said he was considering whether to join Saudi strikes against the rebels, a scenario that could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through a crucial waterway and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf.

Later Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry reported that a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

items: Saudi-led coalition vows retaliation after deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport

blocks.text: The ministry says 91 Yemenis have been killed and 168 injured by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks. It said that 60 per cent of those killed were women and children.
Riyadh shutters airport, schools as Houthis threaten more strikes

The kingdom said Sunday that schools in the capital would hold classes online until the end of the week. Meanwhile, authorities extended an ongoing airport closure until at least 9 p.m. Sunday, according to Flightradar24.
While the Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility for Saturday's attack, they have acknowledged targeting Saudi airports and oil installations in the past.
Another deadly strike on Saudi airport as Houthis escalate attacks

Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the group's military spokesperson, warned "all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces." He wrote on the social media platform X that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina were exempt.

The latest attack on the Saudi airport drew condemnations from Arab countries, including Iraq, Lebanon and Syria, as well as UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
"Attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence," von der Leyen wrote Sunday on X. "They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes."
Details surface about airport fatalities

The attack struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.

A Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said several hospitals were treating the injured.
The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to the Egyptian state-run TV.

The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.

Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56 years old, from Syria's northern Idlib province, and had left during the country's civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed in the attack on the airport, her niece said.
Trump said he would consider joining strikes against rebels
The attack is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies, including the United States, to provide military support for the kingdom.

Shortly after the attack, Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the rebels. "We're going to look at it," he said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
Trump said later Saturday he planned to speak with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Asked if the U.S. might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."
People gather outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid airport in Riyadh on Saturday. (The Associated Press)

A U.S. attack would deepen American involvement in an unpopular regional war that has threatened Trump's Republican party in upcoming U.S. midterm elections. Both Trump and Iran insist the American election calendar has no effect on their decisions on how to end the seven-month-old conflict.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. The airport has no military facilities.

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
Iran can use Houthis to pressure key U.S. ally
The latest fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis comes as negotiations between Iran and the U.S. aimed at ending their war appear to be at a standstill.

Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war. Now, the rebels are helping Iran to pressure a key U.S. ally. Houthi attacks, along with their control of the Bab el-Mandeb waterway, also threaten to add new disruptions to the flow of oil from the region.
The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government.

Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July, when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.

Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb, a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

articles.title: Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted
articles.summary: Film-maker Sue Kim talks about having unprecedented access to K-Pop idol Lisa Manobal at her most candid.

blocks.text: What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?
That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.
The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.
The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.
The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.
Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.
With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.

"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.
The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".
Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.
"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.
Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".
Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.
"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.
"But I did wrong."

It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).
Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.
"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.
"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.
"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."
The incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.
In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head".
"To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".

In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.

That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.
Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece.
"You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says.
"And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."
The film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.
When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.
But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships.
"I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."
As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US.
"Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim.
"In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat.

"Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."
The potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.
In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.
At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.
Kim says that began to change as they filmed.
"I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."

Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.
She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.
On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career.
"Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview.
"And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."
Kim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule.
"But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.
The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted.
"It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim.

"I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."

articles.title: Young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to Myanmar's army
articles.summary: A desperate junta is in a war of attrition against ethnic militias and and civilian resistance.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Authorities in Myanmar have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas, leading to corruption, extortion and abductions
ByGavin Butler and BBC Burmese
You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.
But Zaw Min has no choice.

"I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time.
"People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."

Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.

According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.

Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.
Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.

The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.

blocks.caption: Image caption, An estimated 100,000 young recruits have been conscriptedby the junta since early 2024

blocks.text: Image source, Telegram/@pyithusitt
An estimated 100,000 young recruits have been conscriptedby the junta since early 2024
Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions.

"Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.

The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.
They said they had no comment on the matter.

With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.

The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.
International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.
In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025.
Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law.

"In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.
Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.
Watch: BBC goes into jungle with Myanmar's civil war rebels
"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."
Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time.
"We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."

Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.

The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.
In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.
U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities.
When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.
But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription.
"[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls.

"If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward.
"I also regret placing my trust in my cousin."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ma Moe San Pan says her husband was sold into military service by her own cousin

blocks.text: Image source, BBC Burmese
Ma Moe San Pan says her husband was sold into military service by her own cousin

In the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.
The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.
She does not know where her husband is now.

Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.

Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says.
"Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."

In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department – a branch of the home affairs ministry – and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.

The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison.
BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful.
"Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says.

"They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."

blocks.caption: Image caption, It's been more than a year since Ma Moe San Pan last saw her husband Phyo Wai

blocks.text: It's been more than a year since Ma Moe San Pan last saw her husband Phyo Wai

While conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper – demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population – wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.
So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.

Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".
But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.

It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.
The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".

In addition to the daily anxiety of life in Myanmar, many would-be recruits now fear being forced to fight in a deadly conflict that they not only don't believe in, but actively oppose. This constant threat has fuelled massive internal displacement and severe labour shortages in an already flailing economy, and sent people fleeing to neighbouring countries.
Having spent more than half a decade waging war against its own population, the junta is now wielding the conscription law as yet another tool of subjugation, observers say.
As the MDSI put it in a statement published in June: "The generals have benefited by using military law to make the citizens fight against each other."

articles.title: Dozens reported injured in Yemeni Houthi attack at Riyadh airport
articles.summary:
Saudi authorities yet to confirm strike as government-allied forces in Yemen claim successful offensive to retake Bab al-Mandab strait

Yemen’s Houthis have launched a missile attack on…
articles.byline: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor and agencies

blocks.text: Yemen’s Houthis have launched a missile attack on Riyadh’s international airport in Saudi Arabia, with dozens reported wounded and a witness describing panic in the terminal.

Saudi authorities did not confirm any new attack or evacuation, but one witness reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.
“I was on gate 403,” at the domestic terminal, the witness told Agence France-Presse. “I saw [gate] 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”
A source at a local hospital told the news agency that five people were in intensive care after being wounded at the airport, and “dozens” more had been injured.
The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass and taken to hospital.
Witnesses said people were being evacuated from the airport.

Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi ⁠on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this ​week, leaving four people dead and ‌others wounded, and ‌badly damaging an aircraft.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.

The attack came as forces allied to the UN-recognised government in Yemen claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, but accounts vary as to whether the push has been repelled.

blocks.caption: Fighters from the Southern Giants Brigades clash with Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab strait in Taiz province, 6 October. Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A Houthi spokesperson said forces from the Saudi-backed government based in Aden “were targeted with a large number of ballistic missiles, artillery support and heavy weapons, resulting in the destruction of more than 22 armoured vehicles and the killing and wounding of dozens, including a number of commanders.
“More than 30 ambulances arrived in Aden to transport the dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations.”

By contrast, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said: “Blessed Friday and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al-Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia.”

blocks.caption: The Southern Giants, linked to the STC, are the chief pro-government force fighting around the Bab al-Mandab strait. Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The exposed 5 sq mile (13 sq km) Perim Island straddles the strait, acting as a lookout point for all traffic from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden and towards the Indian Ocean. Aidarous al-Zubaidi, the president of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), one of the main political forces in the south of Yemen, claimed the island and coastal area had been recaptured from Houthi hands.

An official military spokesperson for the UN-recognised government forces qualified the claim, saying only half the area had been recaptured so far. Waddah al-Dabish said newly established Houthi defensive lines had been broken on the land next to the strait, leading to the death of thousands of Houthi fighters.

It is thought that as many as 500 Houthis fighters are stationed on the island, and Saudi Arabia is desperate to be able to report that the strait has been reclaimed to show that the land counteroffensive it launched at the beginning of the week is advancing.

blocks.caption: Southern Giants fighters fire at Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab strait in Taiz province, 6 October. Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The report came as the United Nations’ special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, admitted to the UN security council in New York that Yemen – the poorest country in the world – had lapsed back into full-scale war and said the first victims would be women and children.

The Houthis seized control of the strait two weeks ago and said no Saudi-linked commercial traffic would be permitted to go through the narrow waterway. The Houthis are waging a war to remove Saudi influence from Yemen, and have been mounting missile attacks on Riyadh in support of this objective.

There have been previous premature reports of military breakthroughs by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since it launched its counteroffensive at the start of the week, but the recapture of the land by the strait and Perim Island (also known as Mayyun Island) is a military prize western governments desperately need.

articles.title: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’
articles.summary:
March is first since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful

Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support…

blocks.text: Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them by Israel.

The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine“ as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza.

Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

A ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.

Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to the UK, shared a video from the march on social media. “Three years on, Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank continue, and so does the solidarity of the British people. Louder, bigger, and not going anywhere. Thank you all,” he said. By Saturday afternoon, organisers said 250,000 people were at the march.

The Metropolitan police have imposed conditions on the event – which is organised by the Palestine Coalition, which has organised more than 30 mass demonstrations since October 2023, with a counter-protest by Stop The Hate – to “minimise the risk of serious disruption to communities”.
The Metropolitan police posted on X saying: “The front of the procession has now entered Whitehall where a rally will take place.
“Several arrests have been made so far including a woman and a man with placards declaring support for proscribed organisation Palestine Action.
“We have also arrested a number of protesters on suspicion of criminal damage after they climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.”

The national march is the first held since the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government would take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety. He also told the Commons that settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.

At Labour party conference last month, Miliband appeared to reference the marches, which at their peak regularly numbered hundreds and thousands of people, telling the audience in Liverpool: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.”

Deputy assistant commissioner Carl Galvin said: “We know Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.”
Galvin, who is leading the policing operation this weekend, said the force’s presence on Saturday will be “significant”.
“We will also be using powers under the Public Order Act requiring anyone in the protest area wearing face coverings to deliberately conceal their identity to remove them,” Galvin continued.

The Met have imposed conditions on the march and require the group to travel via Westminster Bridge, York Road, Waterloo Bridge and The Strand on to Whitehall, with a rally concluding by 6.30pm. The force has said that any speeches and music must conclude by 5.30pm.
A counter-protest by Stop The Hate is also taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside New Scotland Yard, some with flags.

The force has also imposed conditions on the demonstration “to minimise the risk of serious disruption”. The demonstrators must remain within a designated area outside the Met’s headquarters, with the assembly concluding at 2.30pm.

Last Saturday, on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas militants broke across the Israeli border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals, killing at least 1,209 people, a small pro-Palestine student demonstration in central London was held.

The Met publicly appealed to those behind the demonstration to “exercise [their] right to protest on a different date” and admitted that finding the organisers had been “frankly difficult”. In the end, it went ahead and about 100 people attended. Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march.
The Palestine Coalition organising the march includes Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War, CND, the Muslim Association of Britain, Friends of Al Aqsa and the Palestinian Forum in Britain.

articles.title: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in Delhi
articles.summary: Thousands of security personnel were deployed in Delhi ahead of the Gen-Z led Cockroach Janta Party protest on Saturday calling for electoral reforms.

blocks.text: Protesters were heard slamming on bus windows following their detention during an anti-government demonstration called by The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi.
The CJP shared a video on social media showing its founder Abhijeet Dipke being detained with other leaders shortly after landing in the capital.
The movement started in May after India's Chief Justice likened some unemployed young people to "cockroaches".
Delhi police denied permission for the demonstration to take place, with tens of thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded.
But the CJP had insisted it would go ahead.
BBC correspondent Azadeh Moshiri, on the ground in Delhi, explains what the latest protest is about.

articles.title: 'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year
articles.summary: Already named the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year, "rage bait" has also been widely adopted in German slang.

image.caption: 'Ragebait' has been selected as the 2026 German Youth Word of the YearImage: Udo Herrmann/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 2026 Youth Word of the Year, "Ragebait," was announced on Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair by publisher PONS Langenscheidt.
The "Jugendwort des Jahres," or German Youth Word of the Year, is an annual campaign that documents the popularity of new slang expressions.
"Ragebait" (in English: rage bait) refers to social media content that is deliberately designed to make people angry, frustrated or morally outraged.

It aims to drive engagement, since the algorithms of platforms like Instagram, TikTok and X reward high-energy interaction. A post that generates a heated debate through angry comments, or that is widely shared due to the emotional reaction it provokes, counts as high engagement, which leads the platforms to push the content to more feeds.
Shortlist also included 'Peak' and 'Crashout'
"Ragebait" was on a shortlist of three words for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year, alongside "Peak" and "Crashout."
All three terms are borrowed from English, demonstrating once again the language's significant influence on German youth culture.
Around one million young people, aged 11 to 20, have voted since August 28 for their favorite term.
"Ragebait" obtained 36.5% of the votes, followed by 33.8% for "Peak" and 29.7% for "Crashout."

"The close result shows that all three terms have a firm place in the vocabulary of generations Z and Alpha," said Artur Raiser, marketing manager at PONS Langenscheidt, in a press statement. "'Ragebait' held a slight lead from the start," but only by a narrow margin throughout the voting period, he added. "It remained an exciting race for us at the publishing house, too, until the very last moment."
Peak crash out
"Crashout" (used by young Germans as "crashout gehen," or "going crash out") originally comes from the English "to crash out," which traditionally means to fall asleep very quickly due to exhaustion.

But in newer internet slang, popularized on gaming and social media platforms, "crashing out" means having an intense emotional breakdown, losing control of one's temper or reacting with sudden, uncontrolled anger or stress. It is often used with a touch of humor, to emphasize that the reaction might be somewhat exaggerated.
As for the other shortlisted word, "Peak," it refers to something that is the absolute best. In German youth slang, it functions like an adjective: "That was peak football" or "that is peak comedy."

PONS Langenscheidt, a publishing company that specializes in language reference works, has been selecting the German Youth Word of the Year since 2008 — originally via a jury, and since 2020 through an online vote. Offensive, racist or discriminatory terms are not permitted. The multi-stage public nomination and voting process for next year's word will start in the summer of 2027.
"Das crazy" was selected last year, while "Aura" was the Youth Word of the Year 2024.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Operations Plan Germany: How the Bundeswehr trains for NATO collective defense
articles.summary: How prepared is Germany for national defense? The answer lies in the Operations Plan Germany. Military exercises such as "Red Storm Charlie" are designed to put these preparations to the test in…

image.caption: The Bundeswehr conducted exercises in HamburgImage: Norbert Schramm/Bundeswehr

blocks.text: In a residential district of Hamburg at midnight, the streets are quiet and deserted. Suddenly, the silence is shattered: Several helicopters circle the night sky, and flashing blue lights illuminate the darkness. A long convoy of vehicles moves through the streets. Soldiers stand atop armored Bundeswehr vehicles, their machine guns at the ready. For local residents, it is an unusual, perhaps even unsettling sight in an otherwise peaceful port city.

"Red Storm Charlie" is the name of the exercise that will bring parts of Hamburg, northern Germany's largest city, to a standstill for three days. The Bundeswehr, police, and civilian organizations are jointly testing how well prepared they are to respond in a crisis.

The scenario centers on a deteriorating security situation on NATO's eastern flank. NATO troops, represented in the exercise by Bundeswehr soldiers, arrive at the port of Hamburg, Germany's largest seaport, before moving eastwards through the Hanseatic city.

Acts of sabotage and demonstrations, also included in the scenario, hamper their advance. With around 1,700 participants, including 500 soldiers, the exercise held in late September 2026, was the largest of its kind to date.

"Red Storm Charlie" forms part of a classified strategy known as the "Operationsplan Deutschland" (Operations Plan Germany). Through this document, the Bundeswehr is preparing for the possibility of a Russian attack on NATO territory. The Operations Plan Germany is an integral element of NATO's broader defense planning and is closely aligned with the Alliance's overall defense framework.
NATO members in Kyiv: 'We stand unwavering with Ukraine'

In the event of war or a major crisis, not only the city of Hamburg but Germany as a whole would assume a pivotal role as a logistics hub for hundreds of thousands of NATO soldiers, weapons, and pieces of heavy equipment. "This is a highly detailed and strictly classified plan that specifies exactly where NATO allies would arrive in Germany, including which ports they would use and which routes would be required for their transit across the country," security expert Aylin Matlé of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) told DW.
Germany as a transit country for NATO troops

The Baltic states are widely regarded as the region where NATO considers a Russian attack most likely. In such a scenario, the alliance would concentrate large troop contingents from its 32 member states there. To reach the region, soldiers from southern and western Europe would need to pass through Germany. "In concrete terms, this means that around 800,000 soldiers and 200,000 vehicles would have to move through our country within six months. Those are the calculations," says Marcel Bohnert, a Bundeswehr officer who contributed to the first version of the Operations Plan.

Speaking to DW in a personal capacity rather than as a representative of the Bundeswehr, Bohnert explained: "We must ensure that soldiers can use our roads and ports safely. That is why we take care of all their needs: We arrange accommodation, provide food, ensure their security, and guide them through our transport network."

The plan also covers transport in the opposite direction, from east to west, including the evacuation of wounded soldiers and civilians fleeing the conflict. Its development was commissioned by Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. As Germany's highest-ranking military officer, Breuer is far from alone in his concern that Russia could target additional countries. Germany is already confronting a wide range of Russian hostile activities, from cyberattacks to acts of sabotage directed against the Bundeswehr.
German spy chief warns of rising Russia threat
Defense Minister Pistorius: 'Moscow is testing our response'

A new dimension of the threat emerged with the attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August. An explosive-laden drone was deployed there and failed to detonate only through luck. The German government holds Russia responsible. "The threat is becoming more tangible. It is serious, acute, and increasingly visible. This is exactly what the Russian president wants. Moscow is testing our response," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told the Bundestag on September 23.

The Bundeswehr is also addressing this threat through the Operations Plan Germany, which is continuously being refined and updated. Lessons learned from exercises such as "Red Storm Charlie" are incorporated into the plan. According to Bohnert, the plan also serves as a deterrent: "We hope to discourage Russia from further aggression by demonstrating our strength through the rapid build-up of military capabilities and the highly organized, swift deployment of forces to the borders."
Roads and bridges need upgrading

How well prepared is Germany for its role as a military logistics hub? Matlé identifies one major vulnerability in the country's ageing and, in some cases, deteriorating infrastructure. Germany, she argues, must address the maintenance and repair of the bridges, roads, and transport routes required for troop movements "far more quickly and comprehensively." "Some of this infrastructure dates back to the Cold War and was not designed to accommodate heavy loads or military equipment."

A further challenge lies in striking the right balance between confidentiality and public involvement. To guard against acts of sabotage, sensitive details such as the precise transit routes for NATO troops must not fall into Russian hands. At the same time, the plan can only succeed through close cooperation between the Bundeswehr and civilian society, including local and regional authorities, the police, and relief organizations. "Parts of the plan must be publicly accessible because we need support from society, as well as from ministries and governments, to make it work," said Bohnert.
Could the AfD pass on sensitive information?

The debate over the confidentiality of the more than 1,000-page document recently resurfaced after the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) emerged as the strongest party in recent elections in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Security experts expressed concern that the party, which is classified in part as right-wing extremist and is regarded as Russia-friendly, could pass information from the plan to Moscow if it were to assume the office of state premier. The Defense Ministry rejected these concerns, noting that no federal state is given access to the complete document. Instead, the sensitive sections of the Operations Plan are shared only in excerpts and strictly on a need-to-know basis.

According to observers, however, the growing number of hybrid threats is underscoring the need for secrecy. During the "Red Storm Charlie" exercise in Hamburg, accredited journalists were not informed of routes or locations until the very last moment because of concerns over potential disruptions and acts of sabotage.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: ‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown
articles.summary:
Authorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral roll

Indian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi

blocks.text: Indian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained tens of thousands of people, including the leader of the youth-led “Cockroach” movement, in an attempt to stop an anti-government protest.

Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll.

The Cockroach movement, as well as opposition parties, civil society and student groups, have alleged that the process of “purifying” India’s voter roll was done to entrench the power of Narendra Modi‘s government, and have called for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw the exercise, to resign.

blocks.caption: Police detain and carry a protester away in Delhi. Photograph: Manish Swarup/AP

blocks.text: Delhi police denied permission for the protest to take place in the centre of the capital, and in the days leading up to Saturday, officials began to barricade roads throughout Delhi. More than 25,000 police and security personnel were deployed across the city, many pulled from other states.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder and leader of the CJP, accused the government of being scared of the young people who were rising up in protest. “The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength but of a leader terrified of his own people,” said Dipke.

On Saturday morning, police boarded Dipke’s plane as it landed at Delhi airport and detained him, alongside several other senior figures in the Cockroach movement. In a video recorded just before police detained him, Dipke said: “If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail, then you have it wrong. Put us in jail if you want … but we will keep fighting to protect the democracy of this country.”

blocks.caption: A protester being detained by security personnel. Photograph: Adnan Abidi/Reuters

blocks.text: Others in the CJP movement were detained across India, with arrests and detentions reported to be in the tens of thousands. One of India’s most popular YouTubers, Dhruv Rathee, who has 33m followers and has become a supporter of the CJP, was among those put under house arrest, while Delhi’s former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal was detained at the protest site.

Student groups, who have also been calling for Kumar to resign, had described the march as India’s “second freedom struggle”, akin to Gandhi’s fight for independence. As police began mass detentions on Friday night, Neha Bora, a student leader at the forefront of the protests, said: “History is repeating itself. Just like in 1942, the arrest of leaders could not stop the Quit India movement; this movement will also not stop.” By Saturday afternoon, Bora had been detained.

Over its 14 years in power, the Modi government has been rigidly intolerant of dissent but few protests have prompted such a draconian nationwide crackdown. In major disruption to travel, all trains arriving into Delhi’s two main stations on Saturday were cancelled for 10 hours and almost 50 metro stations were shut. Delhi’s schools and courtrooms were instructed to go online for the day and hotel owners were told to turn away customers.

blocks.caption: Security personnel chase a protester. Photograph: Manish Swarup/AP

blocks.text: Traffic diversions were in place across Delhi and police checkpoints were set up along the main highways from neighbouring states into the capital, with passengers being stopped and interrogated about their final destination. Delhi police told Uber drivers not to drop people near the protest area and said they were “tracking and stopping” bulk orders on food delivery services to Jantar Mantar.
In Mumbai, housing societies sent out mass WhatsApp messages, telling parents to “mind your kids” and make sure they didn’t attempt to travel to join the protest.

Around Jantar Mantar, which had previously been Delhi’s designated protest site and where the Cockroach supporters had hoped to gather, most of the main thoroughfares were shuttered and barricaded, surrounded by police and paramilitary officers. Riot-control vehicles and trucks fitted with water cannon stood nearby.

Buses were used to transport more than 10,000 people who were detained while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar. Paravin Singhal, a 75-year-old lawyer, said he had left home at 5am and shown his court identity card at checkpoints along the way, only to be stopped about 200 metres from Jantar Mantar.

Singhal said he had come to stand with young people fighting to save the country from a “lawless regime playing with the constitution”. He accused Modi’s government and the election commission of using the revision of electoral rolls to influence future votes.

After voting in elections for 50 years, he said, he had recently been told that his name had been removed from the rolls. “How can this happen to someone who has been voting for 50 years? What is even more disturbing is that the government is taking away our most fundamental right – the right to vote.”

Singhal said he would stay put in the hope that more protesters would arrive. “The government is afraid because young people in this country are awake. They know their rights and are fighting for them. That is why the government is behaving like a dictatorship.”

blocks.caption: Police patrol the streets of Delhi. Photograph: Adnan Abidi/Reuters

blocks.text: Amina Minnath, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, had also travelled to the area with friends. They had left before sunrise and navigated the checkpoints. The police barricading of Delhi, she said, had only strengthened her determination to protest.

“These restrictions show that the government does not care about people’s rights,” she said. “This will not stop us. We may be detained, but we will come back in greater numbers. This will not end in a single day.”

The revision of electoral rolls, in a process known as “special intensive revision (SIR), began last year and attracted criticism from civil society groups and the opposition alliance after it emerged that millions of names were being deleted.

The backlash grew when SIR was held in the state of West Bengal and it became clear that Muslims and other minorities, who traditionally do not vote for Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), were being disproportionately stripped of their vote.

blocks.caption: A protester is detained. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA

blocks.text: Yet it didn’t become an issue of national outrage until late last month, when the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that exposed multiple irregularities in the SIR process, which had been flagged in more than a dozen internal objections but had been unilaterally overruled by Kumar.

Opposition parties, the Cockroach movement and student groups began to call for the resignation of Kumar, who was appointed by a committee led by Modi. This week, India’s main opposition Congress party, also tried to reach Jantar Mantar to protest but were blocked by police, and the Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, was detained twice.

This week, the supreme court ordered the Modi government and the election commission to respond to the allegations. A BJP spokesperson said they had “no base, not an iota of evidence” and accused them of being driven by “an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”.

Saturday’s protest follows the triumph of the Cockroach movement in July, when it led mass protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister. Since then, India’s youth have proved more willing to criticise the Modi regime and have expressed mounting anger at the obstruction of their freedom to protest.

Many, such as Prakhar Vashishth, who is in his early 20s, remained defiant despite the aggression of Delhi police. He had recently been asked to submit additional documents to establish his eligibility to remain on the electoral rolls.
“We are living in extraordinary times, and young people in this country must come out to defend their future,” he said, as he stood near the police barricades around Jantar Mantar.
“This government will go to any lengths to stay in power, even changing election rules or removing people it believes will not vote for it. But they cannot keep us away for ever.”

articles.title: Candidate named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
articles.summary:
Leftwing Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores beats far-right candidate in election in remote district of Andes

A businessman called Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has been elected the mayor of a…

blocks.text: A businessman called Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has been elected the mayor of a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, according to local election data.
The 45-year-old, who shares two of his names with the notorious European dictators, won the race for mayor of Queropalca, in Peru’s central Huánuco region, and will take office on 1 January.
The candidate from the leftwing Ahora Nación party won 229 out of a total of 663 votes in elections on 4 October, according to the national office of electoral processes.
His closest rival, the far-right candidate Gaspar Osorio, received 204 votes.
Flores, who works in freight transportation, had belonged to Popular Force, the party of Peru’s rightwing president, Keiko Fujimori, until 2025, according to electoral authorities.
Despite the name being associated with Germany’s Nazi leader Adolf Hitler, several candidates with the name have won elections in Peru.
In 2021, the doctor Hitler Saavedra Casternoque was elected to parliament for the centrist party Somos Peru.
In 2018, Hitler Alba Sánchez was voted in as mayor of the Andean district of Yungar, saying during his campaign that he was “the good Hitler”.

articles.title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
articles.summary: The Pentagon says the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, but experts suggest officials are reading the country wrong.

blocks.text: They came in their thousands from near and far - men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.

It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heat wave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to the spectators.
By the execution time of 5am, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.
That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.
The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.

Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner;" the local sheriff had died four months earlier, and his widow became the unlikely female replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.
That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in America. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky, and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.

By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.

A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad would be live-streamed.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.
University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked.
"I never imagined [another] public execution," he told BBC.
He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining; it was 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%.
"It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.
It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's nearly certain that millions or more will tune in.
With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment … bring your popcorn, invite your friends".
Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream.

"What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up … to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."

Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's 2002 death, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.
The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution.

"I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."
But the polarisation and rhetoric in American politics may have, in some way, perhaps set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University.

"Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't, and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution; they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"

articles.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
articles.summary: After four years, a Ukrainian man is set to stand trial in Hamburg accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream pipelines.

blocks.text: Image source, Swedish Coast Guard
Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022
BySarah Rainsford
Eastern and Southern Europe correspondent
Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.

Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.
But German police were already closing in on him.

After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.

Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".
Both he and his country have denied any involvement.
Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor
It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.
